Second, report practical efficiency metrics: training speed, memory, and scaling with context length and number of Pushdown layers. Third, provide beam-size sensitivity and perhaps oracle or approximate-search diagnostics for BLIMP/SG scoring. Fourth, clarify the attachment masking and constituent-selection mechanism in the main text. Fifth, temper the downstream claims and present GLUE results as preliminary.

In summary, I think this is a strong and creative paper with a meaningful architectural idea and encouraging empirical results. Its main contribution is not just “syntax helps,” but a specific way of injecting recursive state into Transformer attention without changing the token output space. The evidence on Dyck, SG, BLIMP, and sample efficiency is compelling enough to suggest the idea is real. My reservations are mostly about causal attribution, fairness and completeness of comparisons, and practical overhead. If those issues were better addressed, this would be an even stronger submission.

My overall recommendation is positive. I see this as a worthwhile contribution to the literature on structured inductive biases for Transformers, with clear novelty and promising results, though not yet a fully definitive empirical case.

This paper proposes Pushdown Layers, a modified self-attention mechanism for autoregressive Transformer language models that explicitly tracks recursive structure through a stack-like “stack tape” encoding token depths in an incremental parse. The central idea is elegant: as the model predicts each next token, it also predicts an attachment decision that updates an implicit shift-reduce parse state; the resulting depth information is then injected into attention through additive depth embeddings on keys. The method is positioned as a drop-in replacement for standard self-attention, trained with silver constituency parses, and evaluated on synthetic Dyck languages, sentence-level syntactic generalization benchmarks, a newly constructed parsed Wikipedia corpus, and downstream GLUE-style classification tasks after GPT-2 finetuning.

Overall, I found the paper strong, technically interesting, and well motivated. The problem setting is important: despite the empirical success of Transformers, recursive structure remains a persistent weakness, especially under distribution shift and in low-data regimes. The paper identifies a concrete architectural gap—lack of explicit recursive state tracking—and addresses it with a mechanism that is substantially more structured than ordinary self-attention, yet less cumbersome than prior transition-based syntactic language models that expand the output space with structural tokens. This is a meaningful contribution. The proposed layer is conceptually clean, the paper is generally clear, and the empirical results are broad enough to support the main claims.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the design itself. The stack tape is a clever compromise between full symbolic parsing and unconstrained neural attention. Rather than forcing hard attention masks or requiring the model to emit long sequences of parse actions, the method uses a compact structural state that softly biases attention. This seems like exactly the right level of inductive bias for the stated goal. The illustrations are helpful here: the schematic on page 1 and the worked example on page 4 make the mechanism intuitive, and Figure 2 on page 4 clearly shows how attachment decisions correspond to constituent reductions and depth updates. I also appreciated that the authors provide explicit pseudocode for both the Pushdown attention block and the attachment head in the appendix (pages 14–15), which improves reproducibility and makes the proposal feel concrete rather than merely conceptual.

The paper also does a good job of situating itself relative to prior syntactic language models. The discussion on pages 2–3 clearly explains why prior parsing-as-language-modeling approaches and Transformer Grammars are not fully satisfactory: they increase sequence length, complicate decoding, and often impose hard structural constraints. Pushdown Layers appear to preserve much of the benefit of explicit syntax while avoiding these drawbacks. This distinction is important and, in my view, one of the paper’s main conceptual advances.

Empirically, the results are compelling. The Dyck experiments are a good sanity check and support the core recursion claim. Table 1 on page 5 shows large gains both for deeper nesting and longer-range dependencies, with especially striking improvements at larger dependency lengths and out-of-distribution depths. These synthetic results alone would not be sufficient, but they nicely validate the intended inductive bias.

The sentence-level language modeling experiments are stronger evidence. On BLLIP-LG, the model improves substantially over a standard Transformer LM on BLIMP and the SG test suites, while maintaining similar perplexity. Table 2 on page 7 is particularly persuasive because it compares against both unstructured and structured baselines. Pushdown-LM achieves the best BLIMP score among the listed models and is competitive with or better than prior structured approaches on SG. Figure 3 on page 6 is also informative: the model performs especially well on center embedding and long-distance dependencies, which are exactly the kinds of phenomena one would hope an explicit recursive-state mechanism would help with. That alignment between architectural motivation and empirical gains strengthens the paper considerably.

The WikiTrees experiments further improve the paper by addressing scale and sample efficiency. Figure 4 on page 7 is one of the most convincing plots in the paper: it shows that adding Pushdown Layers to the upper half of a GPT2-small-style model yields markedly better syntactic generalization at 10M, 50M, and 100M tokens, with a substantial sample-efficiency advantage over the baseline. This is an important result because it suggests the method is not merely a niche improvement on small curated corpora, but may actually matter in realistic pretraining regimes where inductive bias can trade off against data scale.

I also liked that the paper goes beyond intrinsic syntax benchmarks and tests downstream transfer. The gains on GLUE-style tasks in Table 3 on page 7 are modest, but still useful as evidence that the architectural change does not only optimize for synthetic syntax metrics. In particular, improvements on RTE, MRPC, and STS-B suggest that the learned structural bias may help sentence understanding more broadly. I would not oversell these gains, but they are directionally encouraging.

The analysis section is another strength. The parsing result in Table 4 on page 8 is surprisingly strong: recovering competitive unlabeled F1 from a language model trained with silver parses suggests that the model is genuinely learning a coherent latent incremental structure rather than merely exploiting the supervision as an auxiliary signal. The attention analysis in Figures 5 and 6 on pages 8–9 is also useful. It provides a mechanistic story for the subject-verb agreement improvements by showing reduced attention to distractor nouns. This kind of analysis is not definitive, but it is exactly the sort of evidence I would want to see for a paper making architectural claims about recursive computation.

That said, there are a few limitations and open questions that should be discussed more carefully.

First, the method depends on constituency parse supervision, and in the larger-scale setting this supervision is silver rather than gold. The paper acknowledges this in the limitations section on page 9, but the dependence is fairly central. It would help to better understand how sensitive the method is to parser quality, annotation scheme, and binarization choices. Since the stack tape is derived from incremental parses, errors in silver parses could propagate into both training targets and the induced attention bias. Some ablation on noisier parses, alternative parsers, or partial supervision would strengthen the practical case.

Second, the computational story is mixed. The paper argues on page 5 that FLOPs are similar to standard self-attention, but memory increases because keys become effectively 3D tensors indexed by destination and source positions. This is an important caveat. In practice, memory bandwidth and implementation efficiency matter a great deal, and the paper itself notes that standard attention is faster on GPUs. I would have liked more concrete runtime and memory benchmarks, especially for the WikiTrees and GPT-2 finetuning settings. Since the method is advertised as a drop-in replacement, practical overhead should be quantified more explicitly.

Third, inference requires approximate marginalization over parses with beam search. This is reasonable, and the paper correctly notes that it avoids some of the complexity of word-synchronous decoding used in transition-based models. Still, beam size 300 for BLIMP and SG evaluation is nontrivial. It would be useful to know how sensitive results are to beam size, and whether the gains persist under smaller beams or greedy parsing. More generally, because the model is trained with supervised attachments but evaluated through approximate marginalization, there is a train-test interface here that deserves a bit more scrutiny.

Fourth, while the paper claims that Pushdown Layers are a drop-in replacement, most experiments do not replace all layers in the same way. For example, the WikiTrees experiment uses Pushdown Layers only in the final 6 blocks, and GPT2-medium finetuning replaces the final 12 blocks. This is perfectly sensible, but it suggests that the best integration strategy may be nuanced. An ablation over which layers are replaced, or how many, would be informative. It might also reveal whether the structural bias is most useful in higher layers, which would be an interesting scientific finding in its own right.

Fifth, the comparison to prior structured models is mostly convincing, but not perfectly apples-to-apples in all places. Table 2 notes tokenization differences for perplexity, and TG lacks a BLIMP number in the table. None of this undermines the main message, but it does mean the empirical superiority claim should be interpreted with some care. If possible, a more standardized reimplementation or evaluation protocol would make the comparison even stronger.

I also have a few smaller technical questions. The attachment decision uses argmax during stack-tape updates at inference time, while training uses supervised attachment probabilities with precomputed tapes. It would be helpful to clarify whether exposure bias from structural decisions is a concern, and whether any experiments were done with sampled or beam-maintained stack states during training. Relatedly, the discussion on page 5 about “attending to hidden states with old memory” raises an interesting mismatch: earlier token representations are computed using depth values that may later become stale as future reductions occur. The paper acknowledges this but does not deeply analyze its effect. Since this is a distinctive property of the architecture, some discussion of whether it harms consistency—or perhaps acts as a useful approximation—would be valuable.

Despite these questions, I think the paper makes a substantial contribution. The core idea is novel and well executed, the empirical evidence is broad and aligned with the motivation, and the work opens an appealing middle ground between purely implicit Transformers and heavily structured symbolic/neural hybrids. In particular, I find the sample-efficiency result on WikiTrees and the strong syntactic generalization gains on BLLIP/BLIMP/SG to be quite compelling. The paper also feels likely to stimulate follow-up work on structured memory in Transformers, supervised or unsupervised stack induction, and syntax-aware scaling.

In terms of significance, I would rate this as more than an incremental architectural tweak. The proposal changes the internal state dynamics of autoregressive attention in a principled way, and it does so with a clear linguistic motivation and measurable benefits. The method is specialized—it is not a universal replacement for all Transformer use cases—but for language modeling and syntax-sensitive generalization it seems genuinely promising.

My recommendation is positive. I believe this paper is worthy of acceptance. To further strengthen the final version, I would encourage the authors to add more detail on runtime/memory overhead, beam-size sensitivity, and ablations over parser quality and layer placement. But these are refinements rather than fundamental concerns. The paper is thoughtful, technically solid, and presents a compelling case that explicit stack-like recursive state can materially improve Transformer language models.

This paper studies test-time adaptation for concept bottleneck models built on top of foundation-model representations. The central claim is that concept-based pipelines are not inherently robust under distribution shift, even when the underlying foundation model features remain useful, and that one can recover both accuracy and better-aligned concept explanations by adapting the concept bank and classifier using only unlabeled target data. The proposed method, CONDA, combines three stages: concept-score alignment (CSA), linear probing adaptation (LPA), and a residual concept bottleneck (RCB) that adds new concepts at test time. Empirically, the paper evaluates across several datasets with low-level, concept-level, and natural shifts, and reports substantial gains over unadapted CBMs, in some cases bringing concept-based performance close to or above feature-based baselines.

Overall, I found the paper interesting and timely. The topic is important: concept bottlenecks are often motivated by interpretability and sometimes by presumed robustness, but the deployment-time behavior of CBMs under shift has been underexplored. The paper’s framing is compelling, especially the observation in Figure 1 on page 2 that concept-based predictions can degrade sharply under both corruption-style and semantic/contextual shifts. The attempt to connect different failure modes to different adaptation mechanisms is also a strength. At a high level, this is a meaningful contribution that could be of interest to both the interpretability and robustness/TTA communities.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the problem formulation and motivation. The authors clearly articulate that there are at least three distinct ways a deployed CBM can fail: the concept mapping itself may be non-robust to low-level perturbations, the concept-to-label classifier may fail under concept-level shifts, and the concept set may simply be incomplete. This decomposition in Section 2.3 is intuitive and useful. It gives the method a principled modular structure rather than presenting adaptation as a monolithic heuristic. I also appreciated that the paper does not overclaim that concepts are automatically robust; instead it explicitly challenges that assumption.

A second major strength is the breadth of empirical evaluation. Table 1 on page 11 covers multiple datasets, multiple shift types, multiple backbones, and three different CBM construction methods. That breadth matters because the proposed method is intended as a general adaptation framework rather than a tweak for one specific CBM instantiation. The results are mixed in places, but that actually increases credibility. In particular, the paper does not hide negative cases, and Appendix F explicitly discusses settings where adaptation can hurt when pseudo-labels are poor or when the unadapted CBM already exceeds the feature-based pseudo-labeling sources. This honesty is appreciated.

The interpretability analysis is also a positive. The Sankey-style visualizations in Figures 4 and 8 (pages 12 and 31) are helpful for showing how concept-to-class weights shift after adaptation. On Waterbirds, the emergence of bird-related residual concepts such as “feathers,” “wings,” and “beak” is intuitively appealing, and the discussion in Section 4.4 gives a plausible story for how RCB can compensate for missing source concepts. The additional analysis in Appendix E, especially the confidence/consistency plots in Figure 6 on page 29 and the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff in Figure 7 on page 30, is thoughtful and goes beyond raw accuracy reporting.

That said, I have several substantive concerns, mostly around methodological assumptions, fairness of comparisons, and the strength of the evidence for the interpretability claims.

My main concern is that the method relies heavily on pseudo-labels derived from non-interpretable feature-based predictors, specifically an ensemble of zero-shot and linear-probing predictions from the foundation model. This is described in Section 3 and on page 7. In practice, this means the adaptation signal comes from the very black-box pipeline that the paper is trying to replace with an interpretable one. That is not necessarily invalid, but it weakens the conceptual claim that the CBM is being adapted “solely” from unlabeled target data in a self-contained way. More importantly, it raises a fairness issue in the headline comparison that CONDA can “align CBM performance with non-interpretable classification.” If the adaptation target is itself derived from those non-interpretable classifiers, then matching them is less surprising. The paper should be much clearer that CONDA is effectively distilling target-domain behavior from feature-based predictors into a concept-based model at test time. Framed that way, the contribution is still interesting, but more precise.

Relatedly, the pseudo-labeling design creates a ceiling and a dependency that complicate interpretation of the results. In several datasets, the adapted CBM approaches LP or ZS performance, but this may simply reflect the quality of the pseudo-label oracle rather than the intrinsic effectiveness of concept adaptation. Appendix D partially acknowledges this and Table 5 on page 28 shows a large gap between current pseudo-labeling and perfect pseudo-labels, especially on CIFAR100-C. However, the main paper still presents the gains somewhat as evidence that the concept bottleneck itself has become robust. A more cautious interpretation is that the method can transfer robustness from the FM-based predictor into the CBM when pseudo-labels are reliable. That distinction matters.

A second concern is the theoretical framing of shift types and completeness. Section 2 introduces low-level shift as preserving the concept-score distribution and concept-level shift as changing concept scores while preserving prediction distributions. These definitions are neat, but they are also somewhat idealized and tightly coupled to the chosen concept mapping h. In practice, whether a shift is “low-level” or “concept-level” depends on the representation and concept bank, not just the data-generating process. For example, Gaussian noise may alter concept scores substantially for one CBM and not another; the paper indeed uses this as a failure mode. So the taxonomy is useful descriptively, but less convincing as a formal categorization of real-world shifts. Similarly, Definition 1 of concept completeness is quite strong and existential, but the paper does not operationalize it beyond motivating RCB. I would have liked either a more modest framing or stronger theoretical development connecting these definitions to the proposed objectives.

A third concern is the CSA objective. The method assumes access to class-conditional Gaussian statistics of source-domain concept scores, namely means and covariances for each class, even though the source data are unavailable at adaptation time. This is stated in Section 3.1 on page 8. In source-free adaptation this may be acceptable if such statistics are stored, but it is still a nontrivial assumption that should be emphasized more clearly in the problem statement and abstract. Moreover, the Gaussian assumption seems fairly ad hoc. There is no evidence that concept-score distributions are approximately Gaussian, nor that Mahalanobis alignment in concept space is the right inductive bias. Since CSA appears to matter mainly for low-level shifts (Figure 3 on page 12), it would strengthen the paper to include empirical validation of this assumption, e.g., calibration of Gaussian fit, comparison to simpler moment matching, or a nonparametric alternative.

A fourth concern is that the ablation evidence does not fully support the necessity of the full three-stage method. Figure 3 shows that under low-level shifts CSA alone can outperform the full method, and under concept-level shifts LPA alone can match or exceed the full method. This is interesting and consistent with the authors’ narrative, but it also suggests that the unified pipeline may be overengineered or at least not robustly beneficial. The paper should discuss whether one can detect the shift type online and selectively activate components. As written, the method seems to pay extra complexity for components that may be unnecessary or even mildly harmful in some regimes. This is especially relevant because the runtime analysis in Appendix B.1/B.2 and Table 3 on page 23 shows pseudo-labeling dominates cost, but the adaptation stages still add overhead.

A fifth concern is about the interpretability claims for residual concepts. The paper argues that RCB discovers meaningful new concepts and improves interpretability. However, the residual concepts are learned directly to improve pseudo-label agreement, with regularizers for diversity and coherence. This does not guarantee semantic meaningfulness. The automatic annotation procedure in Appendix B.2 uses CLIP-DISSECT-style matching against a candidate vocabulary from ConceptNet and accepts labels above a cosine threshold. This is a reasonable exploratory tool, but it is not strong evidence that the learned residual vectors correspond to stable, human-understandable concepts. In fact, Figure 7 on page 30 explicitly shows an accuracy-interpretability tradeoff as more residual concepts are added. I think the paper should tone down claims that RCB enhances interpretability, or provide stronger human evaluation or intervention-based evidence. At present, the evidence supports “some residual vectors can sometimes be annotated plausibly,” which is weaker.

I also have concerns about the fairness and clarity of some empirical comparisons. First, the backbones differ across datasets, and for CIFAR the paper uses FARE2 robust CLIP rather than standard CLIP. This is reasonable for performance, but it makes it harder to isolate the contribution of CONDA versus the robustness of the backbone. The paper does acknowledge that stronger backbones help, but the main message sometimes blurs whether gains come from adaptation or from starting with a particularly robust FM. Second, the CBM baselines are heterogeneous in both concept construction and source-domain accuracy. For example, Yeh et al. (2020) often has much higher source accuracy than the other CBMs, but the paper also notes in Appendix F that its concepts may be less interpretable because they are optimized for accuracy. This complicates the narrative that CONDA improves “concept-based interpretability” across methods. It may improve accuracy across CBM variants, but interpretability quality is not comparably established across them.

Another issue is that the paper’s main table averages CIFAR-C over 15 corruptions at severity 2, but the choice of severity 2 is motivated partly by preserving pseudo-label quality (Appendix C.1, page 24). This is understandable, yet it also means the benchmark is selected to suit the pseudo-labeling mechanism. Appendix F and Table 8 on page 32 show that at higher corruption severity the method can fail badly because the FM pseudo-labels collapse. This limitation should be more prominent in the main paper, because it materially bounds the applicability of the approach. In deployment settings with severe shift, the method may not help.

I found some aspects of the exposition slightly overstated. The paper claims to be the first TTA method for concept bottlenecks with a foundation model backbone “to our knowledge.” That may be true, but the novelty is somewhat incremental at the component level: CSA is inspired by class-aware feature alignment, LPA is pseudo-label fine-tuning with sparsity regularization, and RCB resembles adding residual capacity with coherence/diversity penalties. The novelty lies more in the decomposition and integration for CBMs than in fundamentally new adaptation machinery. I would encourage the authors to present the contribution in those terms.

There are also some technical details that deserve clarification. The notation in Section 2 is heavier than necessary and occasionally obscures the main ideas. The formalization via measurable transformations and push-forward measures is mathematically neat but not really used later in the analysis or proofs, since there are no formal guarantees. The paper might benefit from simplifying this section and reallocating space to empirical diagnostics. Also, the online adaptation protocol uses the same batch for adaptation and prediction, following common TTA practice, but this can sometimes inflate performance relative to stricter evaluation protocols. The paper should explicitly state whether labels are never used for model selection on target data and how hyperparameters were tuned. Table 4 lists dataset-specific hyperparameters, but it is not clear whether these were selected using target validation labels, source validation, or prior heuristics. This matters for assessing realism.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper has real merit. The empirical phenomenon it highlights is important: CBMs can lose much more under shift than one might expect from their source-domain performance, and adapting the concept layer and concept-to-label mapping can recover a substantial fraction of that loss. The modular design is sensible, and the experiments are broad enough to make the work noteworthy. I especially appreciate that the paper includes negative results and limitations rather than presenting a uniformly rosy picture.

To strengthen the paper, I would suggest the following concrete improvements. First, reframe the method more explicitly as source-free target-domain distillation from FM-based pseudo-labels into a concept-based predictor. This would sharpen the contribution and avoid overclaiming autonomous concept robustness. Second, add stronger baselines from the TTA literature applied directly to the equivalent linear model over FM features, and perhaps to the CBM logits, to show that the gains are not simply due to generic pseudo-label fine-tuning. Third, include an oracle study that disentangles the contributions of pseudo-label quality versus adaptation architecture more systematically, beyond Table 5. Fourth, provide more rigorous evidence for interpretability, ideally human evaluation, intervention utility, or stability of residual concepts across runs. Fifth, discuss or develop a mechanism to detect shift type and activate only CSA or LPA/RCB as needed, since the ablations suggest the full pipeline is not always optimal.

I would also encourage a more careful discussion of what counts as a “concept” in the residual branch. If the residual vectors are primarily latent directions that can sometimes be post hoc annotated, then calling the whole model a concept bottleneck may be somewhat aspirational. A distinction between source concepts with explicit semantics and residual latent concepts with approximate annotations would make the interpretability claims more honest and nuanced.

In summary, this is a good paper on an important and underexplored problem. Its main contribution is not a radically new adaptation algorithm, but a compelling formulation of deployment-time failures in FM-based CBMs and a practical framework that often recovers substantial accuracy under shift while preserving some degree of concept-level explanation. The empirical results are strong enough to make the work interesting, but the current presentation overstates interpretability and underemphasizes the dependence on black-box pseudo-labels and backbone robustness. With clearer framing and stronger validation of the interpretability and adaptation assumptions, this could become a solid contribution.

My overall assessment is positive but not unreservedly so. I see this as a borderline-to-accept paper for a strong ML venue: novel enough in problem framing and sufficiently validated empirically, but with important caveats around assumptions, fairness, and interpretability that should be addressed in revision.

This paper studies an important and timely problem at the intersection of interpretability, foundation models, and robustness under deployment shift. The core question is whether concept bottleneck models built on top of foundation model representations can remain both interpretable and accurate after deployment when the test distribution changes. The paper argues, convincingly, that simply inserting a concept bottleneck on top of a strong foundation model does not automatically confer robustness, and that concept-based pipelines can fail in distinct ways under low-level and concept-level shifts. To address this, the authors propose CONDA, a source-free test-time adaptation framework that adapts the concept bank, the concept-to-label predictor, and an additional residual concept bottleneck using only unlabeled target data. Overall, I found the paper to be strong, well-motivated, and technically interesting, with a clear empirical story and a compelling practical message.

The main strength of the paper is that it identifies a genuinely underexplored problem. There is substantial recent work on concept bottleneck models and substantial work on test-time adaptation, but very little on adapting concept bottlenecks themselves after deployment, especially in the setting where the backbone is a frozen foundation model and the source data are unavailable. This is a natural and practically relevant setting. The paper’s framing is therefore valuable in its own right: it highlights that interpretability mechanisms are not static artifacts, but components that may themselves need adaptation under shift. That is a useful conceptual contribution.

I also appreciated the paper’s decomposition of failure modes. In Sections 2.2 and 2.3, the authors distinguish low-level shifts, concept-level shifts, and incomplete concept sets, and connect these to three corresponding failure modes: non-robust concept mappings, non-robust concept-level classifiers, and insufficient concept coverage. This taxonomy is intuitive and helps motivate the three-stage design of CONDA. Even if some of the formalism is somewhat idealized, the decomposition gives the method a coherent structure rather than presenting adaptation as a monolithic heuristic. This is one of the paper’s strongest aspects.

Methodologically, CONDA is well designed. The three components are sensible and complementary. Concept-Score Alignment adapts the concept vectors so that target-domain concept scores better match source-domain class-conditional statistics; Linear Probing Adaptation updates the concept-to-label layer using pseudo-labels while encouraging sparsity; and the Residual Concept Bottleneck adds new concepts to compensate for incompleteness of the original concept bank. This modularity is appealing because it maps directly onto the identified failure modes. The overview figure on page 6 is particularly helpful in clarifying how the source CBM is transformed into the adapted main branch plus residual branch. The method is also reasonably lightweight in spirit: the foundation model remains frozen, and only shallow concept-related components are adapted.

The empirical evaluation is broad and generally convincing. The paper evaluates across multiple datasets representing different shift types: CIFAR10-C and CIFAR100-C for low-level corruptions, Waterbirds and Metashift for concept-level shifts, and Camelyon17 for natural medical-domain shift. It also tests three different CBM construction paradigms: post-hoc concept bottlenecks, unsupervised learned concepts, and label-free concept bottlenecks. This breadth is a major positive. It suggests that the proposed adaptation framework is not narrowly tailored to one specific CBM instantiation. Table 1 on page 11 is especially informative: it shows that unadapted CBMs can indeed degrade substantially under shift, and that CONDA often recovers a large fraction of the lost performance, sometimes bringing concept-based prediction close to or beyond zero-shot and linear-probing baselines. The gains on Waterbirds for the post-hoc CBM and on CIFAR10/CIFAR100 for several settings are notable.

The component-wise analysis is another strong point. Figure 3 on page 12 supports the paper’s central claim that different adaptation components matter for different shift types: CSA is most useful for low-level shifts, while LPA and RCB matter more for concept-level shifts. This is exactly the kind of evidence needed to justify a multi-stage method. I also liked that the paper does not merely report aggregate gains, but tries to explain why those gains arise. The interpretability analysis in Figures 4 and 8 is similarly useful. On Waterbirds, the adapted concept weights shift from background-dominated associations toward more target-relevant patterns, and the residual concepts appear to recover bird-related attributes such as feathers, wings, and beak. Even if automated concept annotation is imperfect, this qualitative evidence strengthens the paper’s claim that adaptation improves not only accuracy but also alignment of explanations with the target domain.

The appendices are substantial and add credibility. The runtime analysis and Table 3 suggest the method is computationally manageable. The hyperparameter ablations in Figure 5 are helpful, especially in showing that the role of the Frobenius regularizer differs across shift types. The pseudo-labeling ablation in Table 5 is also valuable because it makes explicit that pseudo-label quality is a key bottleneck and that stronger pseudo-labeling can further improve results. I also appreciated that the paper includes negative results in Table 8 and a limitations section, rather than presenting the method as universally successful.

That said, there are several issues that should be addressed or at least clarified.

My main concern is the dependence on pseudo-label quality and, more broadly, on the strength of the non-interpretable foundation-model predictors used to generate those pseudo-labels. In practice, CONDA relies on an ensemble of zero-shot and linear-probing predictions from the same backbone, and the paper explicitly acknowledges that when these are poor, adaptation can fail. This raises an important question about what exactly is being adapted: is CONDA primarily transferring the robustness of the feature-based predictor into the concept-based pipeline, rather than discovering a genuinely concept-level adaptation principle? That is not necessarily a flaw, but the paper should discuss this more directly. In some sense, the method’s success may be upper-bounded by the quality of the black-box predictor used as a teacher. This is especially relevant because one of the paper’s headline claims is that CONDA can align CBM performance with non-interpretable classification; if the pseudo-label source is already strong, this becomes more plausible, but also somewhat less surprising.

Relatedly, the comparison protocol could be sharpened. The paper compares adapted CBMs to zero-shot and linear probing, but it would be useful to compare against standard source-free or test-time adaptation baselines applied directly to the feature-based classifier, not only to the CBM. The paper states that improving the FM itself is not the focus, which is fair, but from a systems perspective the relevant question is whether one should deploy CONDA rather than a standard TTA method on the feature-based model. Some of the current comparisons suggest parity with LP or ZS after adaptation, but a stronger baseline would be LP plus a competitive TTA method. Without that, it is hard to assess the cost-benefit tradeoff of interpretability versus direct adaptation.

A second concern is the theoretical formalization. The taxonomy of shifts is useful, but some definitions feel stronger than necessary or somewhat stylized. For example, defining concept-level shift as one where the concept distribution changes but the prediction distribution remains unchanged is conceptually neat, yet real-world shifts may alter both in more entangled ways. Likewise, the completeness definition is intuitive but not operational. I do not think this undermines the paper, since the method is empirical and the formalism is mainly motivational, but the authors should be careful not to overstate the rigor of these definitions. It may be better to present them as idealized abstractions rather than exhaustive characterizations of deployment shift.

A third issue is that the source-free setting still assumes access to source-domain concept-score statistics, namely class-conditional Gaussian means and covariances for CSA. This is a reasonable assumption and much weaker than retaining the source data, but it should be emphasized more clearly in the problem statement and discussion. In some applications, storing these statistics may be easy; in others, especially with many classes or privacy constraints, even this may require justification. The method is not fully source-agnostic in the strictest sense.

There are also some questions about the interpretability claims. The paper argues that CONDA yields concept-based interpretations better aligned with the target data, and the qualitative examples are promising. However, the evaluation of interpretability remains mostly anecdotal or proxy-based. The automatic annotation procedure in Appendix B.2 is clever, but it is still an indirect measure. It would strengthen the paper to include a more systematic human-centered or task-grounded evaluation of whether the adapted concepts are indeed more meaningful, less spurious, or more actionable. For example, one could quantify overlap with known causal attributes in Waterbirds or use intervention-based metrics. As it stands, the interpretability evidence is suggestive rather than definitive.

I also found some of the empirical outcomes a bit mixed, though the paper is commendably transparent about this. In Table 1, CONDA does not uniformly improve every CBM baseline on every dataset; for example, some adapted results for the Yeh et al. model are worse than the unadapted model. The limitations section explains this reasonably well, especially when the unadapted CBM already outperforms the pseudo-label teacher. Still, this suggests that the method may need a confidence-aware gating mechanism or a criterion for deciding when not to adapt, or which components to activate. The component analysis already hints that not all stages are beneficial under all shifts. A practical extension would be to infer the shift type online and selectively enable CSA, LPA, or RCB.

There are a few smaller technical and presentation issues. The Gaussian assumption for class-conditional concept scores in CSA is convenient, but it would be useful to know how sensitive the method is to this modeling choice. The paper cites CAFA-style alignment, but concept scores may be highly non-Gaussian, especially for sparse or semantically heterogeneous concepts. Also, the notation in Section 2 is somewhat dense relative to the rest of the paper, and some readers may find the measure-theoretic framing heavier than necessary. Finally, while the appendices are detailed, the main paper could benefit from a slightly clearer summary of how hyperparameters are selected and whether any target-domain tuning is involved.

Despite these concerns, I view the paper very positively. The problem is important, the proposed solution is novel and thoughtfully structured, and the empirical evidence is substantial. The work makes a meaningful contribution by showing that concept bottlenecks should not be treated as static interpretability wrappers around foundation models, but as adaptive components that can and should evolve under deployment shift. This is a valuable insight for both the interpretability and robustness communities. The paper is also constructive in spirit: it does not merely diagnose failures of CBMs under shift, but offers a practical remedy that often works well across diverse settings.

For improvement, I would encourage the authors to do three things in a revision. First, strengthen the baseline section by comparing against direct TTA on feature-based predictors and by clarifying the role of pseudo-label quality. Second, temper and refine the interpretability claims, ideally with one more quantitative evaluation beyond qualitative visualizations and automatic annotation scores. Third, clarify the assumptions behind CSA, especially the need for stored source-domain concept statistics and the implications of the Gaussian model.

In summary, this is a strong paper with clear novelty, solid experiments, and an appealing central idea. It opens up an important new direction on adaptive interpretability for foundation-model pipelines under distribution shift. I believe it would be a worthwhile contribution to a top-tier ML venue.

This paper presents Agent S, an open framework for desktop GUI agents that aims to “use computers like a human.” The core proposal combines three ingredients: an experience-augmented hierarchical planner, a continual memory mechanism with narrative and episodic memories updated through self-evaluation, and an Agent-Computer Interface (ACI) that uses screenshots plus an augmented accessibility tree and exposes a bounded set of high-level actions. The paper evaluates the system primarily on OSWorld and additionally on WindowsAgentArena, reporting a substantial improvement over prior baselines and claiming a new state of the art on OSWorld.

Overall, I found the paper timely, practically relevant, and reasonably well executed. The problem setting—general-purpose desktop control through GUI interaction—is important and increasingly central to agent research. The paper’s main strength is that it does not rely on a single trick, but instead proposes a coherent systems design that addresses several known bottlenecks in GUI agents: long-horizon planning, grounding, and adaptation to application-specific knowledge. The empirical gains on OSWorld are meaningful, and the ablations suggest that the proposed components each contribute. I also appreciate that the authors release code and evaluate on a second benchmark in a different operating system. At the same time, the paper is more of a strong systems integration paper than a fundamentally new algorithmic advance, and several methodological details and evaluation choices limit how strongly I can assess the claims. In particular, the continual learning setup, the fairness of comparisons, and the exact contribution of each component deserve more careful treatment.

The technical framing is clear. The overview figure on page 4 is helpful: the Manager retrieves web knowledge and narrative memory to produce subtasks, Workers retrieve episodic memory to execute each subtask, and a self-evaluator summarizes trajectories back into memory. The distinction between narrative memory for high-level task summaries and episodic memory for subtask-level action guidance is intuitive and well motivated. Likewise, the ACI design is sensible. The discussion on pages 6–7 about why raw pixel-only grounding and unconstrained code actions are mismatched to current MLLM capabilities is convincing. The dual-input design—using screenshots for semantic understanding and an accessibility tree augmented with OCR for grounding—seems like a practical and effective compromise. The bounded action space in Table 5 on page 15 also appears well chosen for desktop control.

The empirical results on OSWorld are promising. In Table 1 on page 8, Agent S with GPT-4o improves overall success from 11.21% to 20.58%, with especially large gains in Daily and Professional tasks. The bar chart on page 2 and the detailed table on page 8 both support the claim that improvements are broad rather than isolated to one category. The WindowsAgentArena result in Table 4 on page 10 is also encouraging as a cross-OS sanity check, though the gain there is smaller and somewhat uneven across domains. The qualitative examples in the appendix are useful: the successful trajectories on pages 18–20 show that the system can indeed carry out multi-step workflows across applications, while the failure cases on pages 22–23 help ground the error taxonomy.

That said, I have several concerns about the strength of the experimental evidence. First, the main comparisons are against benchmark-reported baselines rather than against stronger reimplementations or matched ablations under identical prompting, inference budgets, and tool interfaces. This matters because Agent S changes multiple aspects at once: planning, memory, retrieval, action space, grounding representation, and likely prompting structure. The paper acknowledges that the WindowsAgentArena strongest model is inaccessible, but on OSWorld the comparison still mixes architectural and interface changes. In particular, the ACI itself appears to be a major intervention, and Figure 6 on page 9 suggests that ACI alone already improves over the baseline. This makes it difficult to isolate whether the gains primarily come from better agent architecture or from a more favorable interface abstraction. The paper does include ablations, but because they are run on a 65-example subset rather than the full benchmark, the conclusions are somewhat less definitive.

Second, the continual memory update setup raises evaluation questions. The paper states on pages 5–6 that Agent S continually updates memory “even during inference” as it encounters new tasks. If the benchmark evaluation proceeds sequentially and the agent is allowed to accumulate experience from earlier test tasks that can help later test tasks, then the reported numbers are not directly comparable to standard static-test evaluation unless the baseline is given an analogous opportunity. This is especially important because OSWorld contains repeated applications and recurring task motifs. The paper should be much more explicit about whether memory is updated across test episodes, whether task order is fixed, whether multiple runs with different orders were tested, and whether any benchmark leakage could occur through environment-aware exploration tasks or web retrieval. The current description leaves too much ambiguity for a top-tier evaluation claim.

Third, the initial memory construction procedure may blur the line between training and evaluation. On page 6, the authors describe self-supervised exploration using environment-independent tasks and “environment-aware tasks” generated from the initial environments of OSWorld and WindowsAgentArena tasks. This is potentially problematic. If the exploration phase uses benchmark initial states to generate related tasks, then the agent may effectively pre-adapt to the test distribution in a way that is stronger than zero-shot evaluation. Even if no ground-truth labels are used, this still constitutes benchmark-specific pre-exposure. The paper should clarify exactly how these exploration tasks are generated, whether they are derived from test instances, and whether a strict separation between memory-building environments and evaluation environments is maintained. Without this clarification, the “state-of-the-art” claim is harder to interpret.

Fourth, the paper’s notion of self-evaluation is interesting but under-validated. The self-evaluator determines whether trajectories are successful enough to store and summarizes them into textual rewards. However, there is little analysis of evaluator accuracy, false positives, or memory contamination. Since the system learns from its own inferred successes and failures without external supervision, one key risk is reinforcing incorrect strategies. The ablation in Figure 7 on page 9 suggests that summarized experiences help, but this does not tell us whether the evaluator is reliable or merely useful on average. A stronger paper would include at least a small manual audit of stored memories, evaluator precision/recall on success detection, or examples where self-evaluation goes wrong.

Fifth, the paper would benefit from more rigorous reporting of statistical uncertainty and computational cost. The benchmark sizes are not huge, and some category-level differences may be noisy. Confidence intervals or bootstrap estimates would help. More importantly, the proposed system adds web search, multiple retrieval calls, hierarchical planning, reflection, and memory updates. This likely increases latency and token cost substantially. The authors themselves note in the conclusion that step count and wall-clock time are unaddressed. Given that practical desktop agents are highly sensitive to latency, this omission is significant. A method that doubles success rate at 10x cost may still be valuable, but readers need that tradeoff quantified.

On the methodological side, I liked the conceptual decomposition into Manager and Worker, but some parts remain underspecified. For example, how exactly are subtasks represented? How often does replanning occur after FAIL? What prompts are used for the Experience Context Fusion and Trajectory Reflector modules? How are retrieval candidates ranked and truncated? How large are the narrative and episodic memories, and how does performance scale with memory size? The formulas on pages 5 and 16–17 are high-level and mostly schematic rather than operational. For reproducibility and scientific clarity, more concrete implementation detail is needed in the main paper or appendix.

The error analysis is a positive aspect, but it could go further. Table 3 on page 10 shows execution errors dominate, followed by grounding errors, and the pie chart on page 21 attributes 46% of execution errors to planning or grounding. This is useful, but the taxonomy is somewhat overlapping: execution errors often seem to be downstream manifestations of planning or grounding failures. A more causal analysis would be stronger, for example separating first-failure causes from propagated failures, or measuring recovery ability after an initial mistake. The failure examples on pages 22–23 are informative and support the claim that grounding remains brittle, especially when accessibility-tree IDs or screen regions are misleading.

I also want to note a few presentation issues. The paper is generally readable, but there are several places where the writing could be tightened. Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence, especially phrases like “uses computers like a human,” which is rhetorically appealing but scientifically imprecise. There are also minor inconsistencies and typos: for example, some notation around episodic versus narrative experience is a bit confusing across pages 4–5 and 16–17, and the references include what appears to be a duplicated AutoGuide citation. The appendix tables are useful, but some detailed per-app results in Table 8 on page 16 are surprising—for instance, Agent S underperforming the baseline on Calc while doing much better overall—and deserve discussion in the main text.

In terms of novelty, I would characterize the contribution as a thoughtful integration of known ideas—hierarchical planning, retrieval augmentation, memory, reflection, accessibility-tree grounding, OCR augmentation, and constrained action spaces—into a strong desktop-agent framework. The novelty lies less in any single component and more in the particular combination and the empirical demonstration that this combination works better than prior baselines. That is a legitimate contribution for a systems-oriented ML paper, but the paper should be careful not to oversell individual modules as fundamentally new. For example, the “textual rewards” framing is evocative, but in practice this is closer to self-generated trajectory summarization for retrieval than to reinforcement learning in a formal sense.

My main suggestions for improvement are as follows. First, clarify the evaluation protocol around memory construction and continual updates, especially whether benchmark test tasks or their initial states are used during exploration and whether memory persists across test episodes. Second, add stronger controlled comparisons on the full OSWorld benchmark, ideally including a baseline with the same ACI but without hierarchical memory/retrieval, and a version with retrieval but frozen memory. Third, report cost metrics: average steps, wall-clock time, token usage, and web-search overhead. Fourth, provide a more careful analysis of self-evaluator quality and memory noise. Fifth, include uncertainty estimates and, if possible, multiple evaluation orders for continual-update experiments. These additions would substantially strengthen the paper.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper makes a meaningful contribution. The problem is important, the system design is sensible, the empirical gains are nontrivial, and the paper includes useful ablations and qualitative analysis. My overall assessment is positive but not unreservedly so: I believe this is a strong applied/agent-systems paper whose claims would be much more convincing with tighter evaluation protocol and clearer separation between training-like memory accumulation and test-time generalization.

Recommendation: weak accept.

The strongest reasons in favor are the practical importance of the problem, the coherent architecture, and the sizable gains on OSWorld. The strongest reasons against are ambiguity in the continual-learning evaluation setup, possible benchmark-specific pre-exposure through exploration, and limited isolation of which components truly drive the gains. If the authors address these issues in revision, the paper would be significantly stronger.

This paper presents Agent S, an open framework for desktop GUI automation with multimodal language models, centered around three main ideas: experience-augmented hierarchical planning, continual memory construction/update, and an Agent-Computer Interface (ACI) that combines screenshots with an OCR-augmented accessibility tree and a bounded action space. The paper evaluates on OSWorld and WindowsAgentArena, reports a substantial improvement over prior baselines, and includes ablations and qualitative/error analyses. Overall, I found the paper timely, well-motivated, and practically relevant. It addresses an important emerging problem—general computer-use agents—and proposes a coherent systems design that appears to improve performance meaningfully. At the same time, some aspects of the empirical methodology and claims would benefit from tighter validation and clearer reporting.

The strongest aspect of the paper is that it tackles a genuinely difficult and important setting: open-ended desktop control across heterogeneous applications, long horizons, and dynamic interfaces. The framing in the introduction is compelling, and the paper clearly identifies three bottlenecks for GUI agents: domain knowledge, long-horizon planning, and grounding/action execution. The proposed decomposition into manager/worker/evaluator modules is intuitive and well aligned with these challenges. The overview figure on page 4 is especially helpful: it clearly shows how the Manager uses web knowledge and narrative memory to produce subtasks, how Workers retrieve episodic experience for execution, and how the Evaluator closes the loop by summarizing trajectories back into memory. This architecture is not merely a loose collection of tricks; it is presented as a reasonably integrated framework.

A second major strength is the ACI design. The paper makes a persuasive case that raw coordinate prediction or unconstrained code generation are both poor interfaces for MLLM-based GUI agents. The proposed dual-input setup—visual screenshot for semantic understanding plus an image-augmented accessibility tree for grounding—is sensible and practically motivated. The OCR augmentation of the accessibility tree, described on pages 6–7, is a nice design choice: rather than only projecting tree information into the image, the system also injects OCR-derived text blocks back into the tree when missing. Likewise, the bounded action space of primitives such as click, type, hotkey, drag-and-drop, and switch-applications seems like a good compromise between expressivity and controllability. This part of the paper is one of its clearest conceptual contributions, and the ablation in Figure 6 supports the claim that ACI materially helps.

The third major strength is the use of experience at multiple levels. The distinction between narrative memory for full-task abstractions and episodic memory for subtask-level grounded experience is well motivated. The manager retrieves high-level guidance, while workers retrieve more concrete execution traces. This is a more structured use of memory than many prior retrieval-augmented agent systems. I also appreciated the self-evaluator idea: summarizing trajectories into textual “rewards” is an interesting way to compress experience into reusable guidance. Even if one may debate whether this should be viewed as analogous to hierarchical RL, the mechanism itself is plausible and practically useful.

Empirically, the headline results are strong. On page 8, Table 1 reports that Agent S with GPT-4o improves OSWorld overall success from 11.21% to 20.58%, with especially large gains in Daily and Professional tasks. The category breakdown in Figure 2 on page 2 and Table 1 suggests the gains are not isolated to one niche domain. The WindowsAgentArena transfer result on page 10 is also encouraging: without explicit adaptation, Agent S improves over the comparable NAVI setup from 13.3% to 18.2%. Given how brittle GUI agents often are to environment changes, this cross-OS generalization is meaningful. The qualitative examples in the appendix are also useful; for instance, the examples on pages 18–20 show the agent handling terminal/git tasks, LibreOffice settings changes, VS Code find-and-replace, Writer formatting, and file recovery from trash. These examples help ground the claims in concrete behaviors.

The ablation section is another positive. Table 2 and Figures 6–7 provide evidence that web knowledge, narrative memory, episodic memory, hierarchical planning, self-supervised exploration, continual memory update, and the self-evaluator all contribute. In particular, the comparison between “Baseline + Retrieval” and “Agent S (ACI-only) + Retrieval” in Figure 6 suggests that retrieval alone is not enough; the interface and planning structure matter. The error analysis is also appreciated. Table 3 on page 10 and the appendix discussion on pages 21–23 show that the authors looked beyond aggregate success rate and tried to categorize failures into planning, grounding, and execution errors. The pie chart on page 21, attributing many execution errors to upstream planning/grounding issues, is informative and points toward future work.

That said, I do have several concerns, mostly around experimental rigor and clarity rather than the overall direction.

My main concern is that the absolute performance remains low, despite the relative gains. A 20.58% success rate on OSWorld is a meaningful improvement over prior baselines, but it still means roughly four out of five tasks fail. The paper is honest about this, and the error analysis helps, but some of the framing occasionally reads stronger than the evidence supports. For example, phrases like “uses computers like a human” are rhetorically appealing but substantially overstate current capability. The system is better described as a promising step toward more capable GUI agents rather than human-level computer use. I would encourage the authors to moderate some of this language.

A second concern is fairness and completeness of the comparisons. The paper compares against reported baselines from OSWorld and WindowsAgentArena under “same input setting” or “similar configuration,” but the exact degree of comparability is not always fully transparent. Agent S uses online web search, self-constructed memories from exploration tasks, OCR augmentation, and a custom ACI. These are legitimate components, but they also introduce additional resources and engineering beyond a plain backbone model. It would help to more explicitly quantify what extra information and compute Agent S receives relative to each baseline. For example, how much of the gain comes from online search versus memory versus interface changes versus simply more prompting structure and more inference calls? The ablations partially address this, but a clearer accounting of test-time budget and external resource usage would strengthen the empirical claims.

Relatedly, the memory construction procedure raises some questions about evaluation protocol. On pages 5–6, the paper states that initial memory is bootstrapped through self-supervised exploration on synthetic tasks, including environment-aware tasks generated from initial environments of OSWorld and WindowsAgentArena. This is interesting, but it also creates a potential concern about benchmark-specific adaptation. Even if no ground-truth labels are used, generating tasks from benchmark environments may still provide a form of exposure to the test distribution. The paper should be much more explicit about whether any exploration tasks are derived from the same applications, websites, or initial states as the evaluation tasks, and whether there is any risk of leakage or overfitting to benchmark idiosyncrasies. This is especially important because the method’s central claim is learning from experience. If the memory is partly built from benchmark-adjacent environments, the distinction between zero-shot generalization and benchmark-specific preparation becomes blurry.

A third concern is the limited scale of the ablation study. The main benchmark has 369 OSWorld tasks, but the ablations are conducted on a 65-task subset, testsub, because of inference cost. This is understandable, but it weakens confidence in some of the finer-grained conclusions. The subset is said to be more balanced than the official small set, which is good, but the sampling procedure is not described in enough detail to assess representativeness. Since many of the paper’s claims hinge on the contribution of individual modules, it would be preferable either to run at least the most important ablations on the full benchmark or to provide confidence intervals / repeated runs on the subset. As presented, some differences may be sensitive to sampling noise.

A fourth issue is that the paper does not report efficiency metrics, despite the architecture being fairly elaborate. The conclusion acknowledges that step count and wall-clock time are unaddressed, and I appreciate that honesty. Still, for an agentic system involving manager planning, web retrieval, memory retrieval, worker execution, reflection, and self-evaluation, cost and latency are central practical considerations. A method that improves success rate by using substantially more model calls or much longer trajectories may still be valuable, but readers need that information to judge the tradeoff. Even simple statistics such as average steps per task, average number of LLM/MLLM calls, average wall-clock time, and token usage would materially improve the paper.

I also found some methodological details underspecified. The retrieval setup uses text-embedding-3-small, but the paper does not say much about memory size, retrieval top-k, prompt lengths, or how often retrieved experiences are stale or contradictory. The self-evaluator is central to the continual learning story, yet its reliability is not independently validated. Since the evaluator determines what gets stored as successful or failed experience “without any human feedback or ground truth information,” errors in self-assessment could compound over time. The ablation “w/o Self-Evaluator” replaces summaries with full trajectories, but that does not isolate evaluator correctness from summarization format. A more direct analysis of evaluator precision/recall on a labeled subset would be useful.

There are also some presentation issues. The paper is generally readable, but several claims could be sharpened. The analogy to hierarchical reinforcement learning on page 5 is suggestive, though somewhat loose; no reward optimization or policy learning is actually performed in the standard RL sense. I would recommend presenting this more cautiously as an inspiration rather than a close formal correspondence. Some notation is also inconsistent or lightly defined in places, and there are minor writing issues throughout. These are not major obstacles, but polishing would help.

One empirical detail that stood out is the uneven per-domain behavior. Table 8 on page 16 shows strong gains in OS, Writer, VLC, Thunderbird, VS Code, and GIMP, but Calc performance appears worse than the baseline (2.13 vs 4.26). Similarly, Table 4 and Table 9 for WindowsAgentArena show zeros in some domains/apps. This does not invalidate the overall contribution, but it suggests the method may be particularly effective in some interface regimes and weak in others. The paper would benefit from a more explicit discussion of where the architecture helps most and why. For example, does hierarchical planning mainly help knowledge-intensive tasks, while ACI helps dense UI grounding tasks? Does web retrieval help browser and office tasks more than system utilities? The current analysis hints at this but does not fully unpack it.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper makes a meaningful contribution. The problem is important, the system design is thoughtful, and the empirical gains are substantial enough to merit attention. In particular, I view the ACI formulation and the multi-level experience retrieval/planning design as the most valuable takeaways. Even if some components are engineering-heavy and the absolute success rates remain modest, this is the kind of systems paper that can move the field forward by showing what combinations of planning, retrieval, memory, and interface abstraction actually matter in realistic desktop environments.

To strengthen the paper further, I would suggest the following concrete revisions. First, clarify the memory bootstrapping protocol and explicitly rule out benchmark leakage as much as possible. Second, report efficiency/cost metrics and, if feasible, normalize comparisons by inference budget. Third, expand ablation reporting, ideally with confidence intervals or repeated runs, and if possible run a subset of key ablations on the full OSWorld test set. Fourth, provide a more direct analysis of the self-evaluator’s quality and the long-term effects of continual memory updates. Fifth, moderate the strongest anthropomorphic claims and better characterize the current limitations suggested by the 20% success rate and the failure taxonomy.

In summary, this is a strong and relevant paper on GUI agents. It proposes a coherent framework with clear architectural ideas, demonstrates sizable gains on a challenging benchmark, and includes useful ablations and failure analysis. The main weaknesses are around evaluation protocol clarity, efficiency reporting, and the still-limited absolute performance. Nevertheless, I believe the paper is a worthwhile contribution and likely to be of broad interest to researchers working on multimodal agents, computer-use assistants, and interactive AI systems. My overall assessment is positive.

This paper studies privacy-preserving activation steering for LLM alignment. The core idea is simple and appealing: compute standard mean steering vectors from paired positive/negative demonstrations, clip and normalize per-example activation differences, and add Gaussian noise so that the released steering vectors satisfy differential privacy. The resulting method, PSA, is then used at inference time exactly like ordinary activation editing, with the important benefit that once the private steering vectors are released, arbitrarily many downstream generations incur no additional privacy cost by post-processing. The paper also proposes what the authors describe as the first membership inference attack tailored to activation steering, based only on generated text rather than token probabilities, and evaluates both utility and empirical privacy across several alignment behaviors and multiple open-source LLM families.

Overall, I find the paper timely, well motivated, and potentially impactful. Activation steering is increasingly used as a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning, and the privacy implications of constructing steering vectors from sensitive demonstrations are indeed underexplored. The paper’s main conceptual contribution is straightforward but meaningful: privatize the steering vectors themselves rather than the model training process. This is a natural fit for differential privacy, and the offline nature of the mechanism is practically attractive. The empirical scope is also fairly broad: seven behavioral datasets, several model families, multiple utility metrics, and an empirical privacy audit. I think the paper makes a credible case that privacy for activation editing is an important problem and that a simple DP mechanism can work surprisingly well.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the clarity of the privacy framing. The setup in Sections 3 and 4 is easy to follow, and Figure 1 on page 2 and Figure 2 on page 5 communicate the two-phase workflow effectively: first generate private steering vectors from paired demonstrations, then use them for unlimited private generation. The post-processing argument is standard but important here, and the paper correctly emphasizes that the privacy budget is paid once when releasing the steering vectors, not per query. This is a genuine practical advantage over many inference-time privacy mechanisms. I also appreciated that the paper explicitly discusses why activation editing may still leak information even though it is not conventional fine-tuning.

The empirical evaluation on alignment benchmarks is encouraging. Figure 3 on page 7 shows that PSA generally tracks non-private mean steering closely and usually remains clearly above zero-shot performance for Llama-2, Mistral, and Qwen across the seven behaviors. The scaling result in Figure 4 on page 9 is also interesting: the privacy-utility gap appears to shrink with model size, at least on the Refusal dataset for the Qwen family. If robust, this is an important practical message, since many real deployments will use larger instruction-tuned models. The MMLU results in Table 5 on page 9 suggest only modest degradation in general capabilities, which helps support the claim that PSA does not catastrophically distort the model outside the target behavior.

That said, I have several concerns, some of them substantial.

My main concern is that the privacy accounting and mechanism specification are underdeveloped relative to the claims. The paper states in Algorithm 1 on page 5 that the private steering vector is computed as the average of clipped/scaled difference vectors plus Gaussian noise with standard deviation sigma = 2 sqrt(2 ln(1.25/delta)) / (n epsilon). This formula appears to assume sensitivity 2/n, presumably because neighboring datasets can differ in one paired demonstration and each clipped vector has norm at most 1. That is plausible, but the paper should derive this explicitly and carefully. As written, the notation is a bit sloppy: the Gaussian mechanism in Fact 2.1 on page 3 is written as adding N(0, sigma^2), which for a vector-valued output is ambiguous. Is the noise isotropic Gaussian N(0, sigma^2 I_d)? Since the steering vectors live in high-dimensional activation space, this matters. More importantly, the privacy guarantee is stated as (|S| epsilon, |S| delta)-DP by basic composition across layers, but the mechanism releases multiple high-dimensional vectors, one per selected layer. If the same example contributes to all selected layers, then composition is indeed needed, but the paper should be more explicit about whether the per-layer epsilon values in Table 2 are chosen independently or derived from a fixed total budget. Right now the presentation mixes “per-layer epsilon” and “total epsilon” in a way that is easy to misread.

Relatedly, the experimental privacy setup fixes the noise standard deviation to 0.02 and then reports the resulting theoretical epsilon values in Table 2 on page 7. This is a somewhat unusual presentation for a DP paper. Typically one fixes a target privacy budget and calibrates noise accordingly. Here, because sigma is fixed across datasets and models, epsilon varies with n and perhaps implicitly with clipping. That is not wrong, but it weakens the privacy-utility story because the comparisons are not made at matched privacy budgets. In particular, some datasets have epsilon around 2 while others are as high as 6.6 total, which is a much weaker guarantee. The paper repeatedly says PSA achieves DP “with minimal loss in performance,” but the utility numbers are aggregated across quite different privacy regimes. A stronger evaluation would sweep epsilon directly and compare utility as a function of privacy budget, ideally against alternative DP baselines.

A second major concern is that the empirical privacy attack, while novel and interesting, is narrow and somewhat stylized. The canary-based MIA in Section 6 inserts synthetic anchor-target pairs into demonstrations and then checks whether the steered model preferentially emits the target when prompted with the anchor. This is a reasonable first audit, but it is closer to a targeted canary extraction test than a general membership inference attack on natural demonstrations. The attack depends on specially constructed synthetic entities, repeated sampling at temperature 0.8, and threshold tuning that differs by model (tau = 40 for Llama-2 and 70 for Qwen, page 10). It demonstrates that non-private steering can encode and reveal synthetic associations, but it does not yet establish how vulnerable activation steering is to realistic MIAs on ordinary private data. The paper should be more careful in its claims here. Calling this “the first MIA for activation editing” is probably fair, but the broader implication that PSA protects against membership inference in realistic settings is less well supported.

The empirical epsilon computation in Section 6 also deserves more scrutiny. The paper uses FPR and FNR from the attack to derive an empirical epsilon, following prior auditing work. This is fine as an audit heuristic, but it is not a direct estimate of the true privacy loss of the mechanism; it is only with respect to a particular adversary and test. The paper does mention that theoretical bounds are conservative, but some of the wording risks overinterpretation. For example, saying that empirical epsilon is lower than theoretical epsilon “suggesting stronger protection with PSA in real-world settings” is too broad given the narrow attack family. It would be better to say that under this specific canary-based audit, the observed leakage is lower than the worst-case DP bound.

A third concern is the strength of the utility evaluation itself. The behavioral datasets are inherited from prior work and are useful for controlled steering experiments, but they are fairly artificial binary-choice tasks. The paper does include open-ended generation evaluation using GPT-4 as a judge, which is good, but Table 3 on page 8 raises questions. For some behaviors, the scores are extremely low across all methods, especially AI Coordination and Sycophancy, making it hard to interpret practical significance. Also, the paper does not report variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests anywhere in the main results. Since the differences between Mean Steering and PSA are often small, it is difficult to know whether they are meaningful or within run-to-run noise. This is especially important because the method itself is randomized. Were the reported PSA numbers averaged over multiple noise draws, or from a single sampled steering vector? The paper does not clearly say. If only one draw was used, the results may be unstable.

The choice of baselines is another weakness. The paper compares PSA mainly to zero-shot, mean steering, and PCA steering. That is a reasonable starting point, but for a privacy paper I would have liked at least one stronger privacy-aware baseline, even if adapted from adjacent settings. For example, a simple non-DP clipping-only baseline, or a mechanism that privatizes a lower-dimensional projection of the steering vectors, or a DP variant of PCA steering, would help isolate whether the proposed mean-based privatization is especially effective. The appendix does include clipping-only ablations on pages 20–21, but these are not integrated into the main comparison. More broadly, the paper’s claim of being the first DP activation editing method is plausible, but the empirical case would be stronger if it compared against more than two non-private steering methods.

There are also some methodological ambiguities. The paper says on page 6 that “the noisy vectors are generated by adding Gaussian noise with 0.02 standard deviation,” but because the vectors are normalized by clipping threshold and live in different layer dimensions across models, it is not obvious that a fixed sigma is comparable across settings. The clipping threshold itself is treated as a hyperparameter estimated from public data, but the main text does not specify how it was chosen in the reported experiments. The appendix ablation on pages 20–21 suggests utility is sensitive to clipping threshold, so this choice matters. Similarly, the selected layers are said to be the five middle layers (11–15) for 7B models in Table 2, but it is unclear whether the same relative layer positions are used for smaller models and all model families, and whether this was tuned per behavior. Since steering performance is known to depend strongly on layer choice, more detail is needed for reproducibility and for assessing fairness of comparisons.

I also found some of the qualitative examples a bit awkward. For instance, the hallucination example in Table 11 on page 19 appears to show both Mean Steering and PSA producing clearly false content, which is consistent with the benchmark’s framing but makes it hard to understand whether lower GPT-4 hallucination scores correspond to better factuality in a practical sense. More generally, because the behaviors include unusual axes like AI Coordination and Survival Instinct, the paper would benefit from a clearer discussion of which results should be interpreted as safety-relevant versus merely diagnostic. This matters because “alignment” is used broadly throughout, but some of these axes are more speculative than others.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper has real merit.
