The problem is novel, the proposed solution is elegant, and the empirical results are promising enough to justify publication if the claims are tightened and the presentation improved. In particular, the paper would be significantly stronger with the following revisions.

First, strengthen the DP exposition. Provide a formal theorem with a complete sensitivity derivation for the vector-valued mechanism, explicitly state the neighboring relation on paired demonstrations, and clarify the exact covariance of the added Gaussian noise. Also explain how the per-layer and total privacy budgets are allocated in experiments, and consider reporting results as utility versus target epsilon rather than fixing sigma.

Second, improve the empirical rigor of the utility evaluation. Report averages over multiple PSA noise draws with standard deviations or confidence intervals. If possible, include significance testing for the gap between Mean Steering and PSA. Clarify how clipping thresholds and layer subsets were selected, and whether any public validation data was used.

Third, temper and broaden the privacy audit claims. The canary-based attack is a useful contribution, but it should be framed as a targeted extraction-style MIA rather than a comprehensive privacy evaluation. If feasible, add at least one more attack variant on naturalistic demonstrations or paraphrased canaries, and analyze sensitivity to temperature, threshold, and number of samples. It would also help to compare against a clipping-only non-DP baseline in the privacy audit.

Fourth, expand the discussion of limitations. The appendix briefly notes that only mean steering and monolingual settings are considered. I would add that the current evaluation does not address adaptive adversaries with white-box access to steering vectors, nor does it study whether private steering vectors can leak aggregate sensitive attributes even when individual membership is protected.

In summary, I view this as a good and original paper with a simple but meaningful technical contribution, solid motivation, and encouraging experiments, but also with some important gaps in privacy accounting clarity, empirical rigor, and attack realism. If accepted, it would likely stimulate useful follow-up work on privacy for inference-time alignment methods. My overall assessment is positive but not unreserved: the paper is above the bar on novelty and relevance, and probably on empirical usefulness, but it would benefit from a more careful and precise treatment of both the DP guarantees and the empirical privacy claims.

This paper studies a timely and important problem: how to obtain privacy guarantees for inference-time activation steering of large language models when the steering demonstrations themselves are sensitive. The paper proposes PSA, a simple differentially private steering method that clips per-example activation-difference vectors and adds Gaussian noise to the resulting steering vectors, then uses these privatized vectors during generation. It also introduces what the authors describe as the first membership inference attack tailored to activation editing, based only on generated text rather than token probabilities. Overall, I found the paper interesting, well motivated, and potentially impactful. The central idea is technically straightforward, but that is also one of its strengths: it is easy to understand, easy to implement, and addresses a genuine gap in the literature.

The main contribution is clear from the outset and remains coherent throughout the paper. The motivation in the introduction is compelling: activation editing is increasingly used as a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning, especially when organizations want to adapt models using their own data, yet the privacy implications of such steering have been largely ignored. Framing the problem around private paired demonstrations is natural, and the paper makes a convincing case that even though activation editing is “training-free,” it can still leak information about the alignment set. I think this is an important conceptual contribution in itself. The paper also does a good job of positioning itself relative to prior work on DP for fine-tuning and in-context learning, making the novelty of the activation-editing setting quite clear.

Methodologically, PSA is elegant. The algorithm on page 5 is simple: compute per-example activation differences, clip and normalize them, average them, and add Gaussian noise. The privacy argument is correspondingly clean. The discussion on pages 5–6 about why privatizing the steering vectors offline allows infinitely many downstream queries at no additional privacy cost is one of the strongest aspects of the paper. This is a practically meaningful distinction from many interactive DP settings. The use of composition across selected layers is also intuitive and well explained. I appreciated that the paper does not oversell the method as a new complex mechanism; instead, it emphasizes that a simple DP construction can already work well in this setting.

The empirical evaluation is broad. The paper covers seven alignment-relevant behaviors, four model families, and multiple model sizes. Figure 3 on page 7 is especially useful: it shows that PSA generally tracks non-private mean steering closely while consistently improving over zero-shot performance on most tasks for Llama, Mistral, and Qwen. This breadth gives confidence that the method is not narrowly tuned to a single benchmark or model. The scaling analysis in Figure 4 on page 9 is also valuable, since it suggests that the privacy-utility tradeoff improves with model size. That is an intuitively plausible and practically relevant finding.

I also liked that the paper evaluates more than just the target alignment metric. The MMLU results in Table 5 on page 9 suggest that PSA has limited impact on general capabilities, which is important because steering methods can sometimes distort unrelated behavior. The open-ended generation analysis using GPT-4 as a judge, reported in Table 3 on page 8 and illustrated with examples in Tables 10–16 on pages 19–20, further supports the claim that privatization does not dramatically degrade output quality. The qualitative examples are helpful and, in several cases, PSA outputs are indeed very similar to non-private mean steering outputs.

The privacy auditing section is another strong point. The proposed canary-based MIA is well matched to the activation-editing setting, where standard loss-based attacks are less natural. The setup on pages 9–10 is clearly described, and Table 7 on page 10 provides a useful comparison between non-private steering and PSA. The empirical epsilon values being below the theoretical bounds is unsurprising but still reassuring. More importantly, the attack demonstrates that non-private steering can leak membership information in a measurable way, which strengthens the paper’s motivation and makes the DP intervention feel necessary rather than merely formal.

That said, there are several limitations and points that would benefit from clarification.

First, while the privacy proof sketch is intuitive, the presentation is somewhat informal in places, and I would have liked a more careful treatment of sensitivity and noise calibration. In Algorithm 1 on page 5, the noise scale is given as sigma = 2 sqrt(2 ln(1.25/delta)) / (n epsilon), which appears to assume unit-bounded clipped vectors and neighboring datasets differing in one paired demonstration. This is plausible, but the exact adjacency notion and the factor of 2 should be stated more explicitly in the main text. Since each record contains both a positive and negative completion, the sensitivity depends on whether replacing one paired record changes the average by up to 2/n after clipping; I believe that is what the algorithm is using, but the derivation should be made explicit. This is not a fatal issue, but for a paper centered on formal privacy guarantees, precision here matters.

Second, the experimental privacy setting is somewhat narrow. The main MIA evaluation appears to focus on the hallucination dataset and two 7B models. Since the paper makes broad claims about privacy-preserving steering across behaviors and model families, it would strengthen the work to show whether the same empirical privacy trends hold for at least a few additional datasets, especially ones with smaller n and therefore weaker theoretical epsilon, such as corrigibility or AI coordination. The current results are still useful, but broader privacy auditing would make the empirical story more complete.

Third, some implementation choices are fixed rather than systematically explored in the main paper. For example, page 6 states that noisy vectors are generated with Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.02 and delta = 1/(5n), yielding epsilon values around 2 for larger datasets and up to 6.6 for smaller ones. This is reasonable, and the appendix ablations on pages 20–21 are helpful, but the main paper would benefit from a clearer explanation of how this operating point was selected and whether it is close to optimal. Similarly, the choice of steering layers seems inherited from prior work, but a more explicit layer-selection rationale or sensitivity analysis in the main text would improve reproducibility and interpretability.

Fourth, the evaluation protocol using GPT-4 as a judge is acceptable but not entirely satisfying. The prompts on page 18 are clearly documented, which I appreciate, but the paper does not discuss inter-run variance, prompt sensitivity, or whether human evaluation was considered for at least a small subset. Since some of the reported differences are small, especially between mean steering and PSA, it would be useful to know how stable these judgments are. This is a common issue in current LLM evaluation papers, so I do not view it as a major flaw, but it is worth acknowledging.

Fifth, there are a few places where the interpretation of results could be more careful. For instance, the claim on page 8 that PSA sometimes improves over non-private steering because DP noise may align the model in a better direction is plausible, but speculative. It would be better framed as an observation rather than an explanation unless supported by additional analysis. Likewise, the statement that larger models are less sensitive because they already contain sufficient alignment-related knowledge is reasonable but remains a hypothesis.

I also have a few smaller concerns. The paper focuses on mean steering and PCA steering baselines, which are appropriate, but the broader activation-editing literature now includes more sophisticated methods. The authors acknowledge this in the appendix limitations section on page 23, but including at least one stronger recent baseline in the main experiments would make the comparison more convincing. In addition, the paper’s threat model is primarily membership privacy for the demonstration set; it would help to discuss more explicitly whether PSA also mitigates extraction of semantic content beyond membership, and what kinds of attacks remain out of scope. Finally, some tables and claims would benefit from confidence intervals or repeated-run statistics, especially because generation with temperature and DP noise both introduce randomness.

Despite these issues, I think the paper is strong overall. Its novelty is real: bringing differential privacy to activation steering is a meaningful contribution, and the paper does more than just add a standard mechanism by also proposing an empirical privacy audit tailored to the setting. The method is simple but well chosen, the experiments are extensive, and the results support the central claim that useful steering can be retained under formal privacy guarantees. I also think the paper is likely to have practical impact because the approach is lightweight and deployable: privatize the steering vectors once offline, then reuse them indefinitely.

My main suggestion for improvement would be to tighten the formal exposition around sensitivity and adjacency, expand the empirical privacy evaluation beyond one dataset, and add uncertainty estimates for the evaluation metrics. None of these require changing the core method, and addressing them would substantially strengthen the paper.

In summary, I view this as a valuable and well-executed paper on an underexplored but increasingly important problem. It identifies a genuine privacy risk in activation editing, proposes a clean DP solution, and backs it up with broad experiments and a novel attack methodology. I am positive on the paper and think it would make a worthwhile contribution to the conference.

This paper studies an important and timely problem: how users can audit black-box LLM APIs to determine whether an endpoint is actually serving the claimed model distribution, or whether it has been altered through quantization, watermarking, finetuning, implementation differences, or silent updates. The paper formalizes this as a two-sample hypothesis testing problem, “Model Equality Testing,” and proposes kernel MMD-based tests, with a particular emphasis on a simple Hamming string kernel over completions. The empirical study is extensive: the authors compare several candidate tests in simulation, examine robustness across distortions and prompt distributions, and then audit 31 commercial endpoints serving Llama-family models. The headline findings are strong and practically relevant: the Hamming-MMD test appears substantially more sample-efficient than several natural baselines, and the audit flags a nontrivial fraction of commercial endpoints as distributionally different from Meta’s released weights.

Overall, I found the paper interesting, well-motivated, and potentially impactful. The problem formulation is clean and useful, and the paper makes a compelling case that benchmark-style auditing is too narrow for many real users. The empirical results are also striking, especially the API audit in Section 5 and the distance visualizations in Figures 3–4 and Appendix C.8. The work is also commendably practical: it releases code and a large completion dataset, and the methodology only requires sample access rather than logprobs. I think this paper has the ingredients of a strong conference contribution. At the same time, there are several methodological and interpretational issues that should be clarified or strengthened before I would be fully convinced by the strongest claims.

The main strength of the paper is the problem framing. Casting API auditing as a distribution equality test is elegant and general. It unifies several practically important questions: faithfulness to open weights, drift over time, and substitution with another model. This is a better fit than accuracy-only auditing for long-form generation, code, and other settings where users care about the full output distribution rather than just greedy correctness. I also appreciated the discussion in Section 3 that kernel choice determines semantics: this is exactly the right lens for understanding why a coarse feature map may miss meaningful differences while a universal kernel may be too sparse in the small-sample regime.

A second major strength is the empirical comparison of tests. The paper does not simply propose MMD in the abstract; it compares Hamming-MMD against one-hot MMD, all-substrings MMD, and classical multinomial-style tests such as L1 and chi-squared. The sample complexity plots on page 6 are persuasive: the Hamming kernel seems to dominate in the low-sample regime that matters for practical auditing. The robustness-to-length result is also important. Since completion spaces explode combinatorially with length, showing that the Hamming kernel degrades more gracefully than one-hot or multinomial tests is a meaningful contribution.

The API audit itself is the most compelling part of the paper. Table 1 on page 9 and the summary in Figure 1 show that 11 of 31 endpoints are flagged. This is a concrete, policy-relevant result. The paper goes beyond binary rejection and estimates effect sizes via MMD, which is valuable because statistical significance alone can be misleading at scale. The observation that some provider deviations are as large as swapping in a different model family is especially notable. The qualitative examples in Box 2 and Appendix D help ground these findings, and the provider-to-provider distance plots in Figure 4 and Appendix C.8 are informative.

That said, my main concern is that the paper’s strongest empirical conclusions depend heavily on one particular kernel whose statistical meaning is limited. The authors are transparent that the Hamming-MMD is only a pseudometric, not a metric, and Appendix A.1 explicitly shows that it only captures stacked token-position marginals rather than the full joint distribution. This is not a minor technicality. It means the test can fail to distinguish distributions that differ in higher-order dependencies while sharing the same per-position marginals. In other words, the method is powerful for some distortions but not a general solution to model equality. The paper acknowledges this, but the framing and conclusions sometimes read more broadly than warranted. I think the paper should more clearly distinguish “detecting many practically relevant distortions” from “testing equality of model distributions” in the full statistical sense. As written, the title and some claims risk overstating what the chosen test can certify.

Relatedly, the kernel selection is almost entirely empirical. That is acceptable to some extent, but the paper would be stronger with more theory or at least more structured analysis of when Hamming-MMD should be expected to work. For example, quantization and watermarking often perturb local token preferences, so a positionwise kernel is plausible. But for finetuning or implementation changes, why should Hamming similarity be the right inductive bias? The fp16 results in Figure 2 already show a failure mode: the test has much lower power there. This suggests the method is sensitive to the geometry of the distortion, not just its magnitude. A more principled discussion of the alternatives the kernel is and is not suited for would improve the paper.

A second concern is the calibration and interpretation of the API audit. In Section 5, the authors define a composite null over fp32 and fp16 reference distributions and reject only if both pairwise tests reject. This is conservative, which is good for false positives, but then they add another layer of aggregation: they repeat tests over ten samples and “fail endpoints if the average rejection rate is at least 0.5.” This latter rule is much less standard statistically, and I did not see a formal justification for its operating characteristics. What false positive rate does this induce overall? How sensitive are the conclusions to the 0.5 threshold, the number of repeats, or the choice of alpha? Since the paper’s most visible claim is that 11/31 endpoints differ from reference weights, the decision rule deserves a more careful treatment. At minimum, I would like confidence intervals over endpoint failure rates, or a sensitivity analysis showing how many endpoints are flagged under nearby thresholds.

More broadly, the audit results may conflate provider-side model changes with other sources of mismatch. The paper notes some of these issues, but they remain important. First, matching chat templates is tricky; Appendix B.1 mentions that the authors used the Llama-3 template for Llama-3.1 because it better matched API token counts at the time. This is reasonable, but it also means the “reference distribution” is partly an inferred implementation choice rather than a canonical ground truth. Second, APIs may differ in undocumented system prompts, stop conditions, tokenizer handling, safety filters, or post-processing. Third, the data collection spans multiple dates for some providers, sometimes over weeks, as shown in Tables 2–6. If an endpoint drifts during collection, the sampled distribution is itself a mixture. Since the paper’s framing includes temporal drift as a target phenomenon, this is not fatal, but it complicates interpretation of a rejection as “this provider modified the model.” The paper should be more explicit that the audit detects endpoint-level distribution mismatch, not necessarily weight-level modification alone.

I also have some reservations about the prompt distributions used in the simulation study. The Wikipedia continuation task is a reasonable long-form benchmark, but it is still a fairly narrow slice of behavior. The prompts are 100-character snippets from multilingual Wikipedia, and the main simulation uses only 25 prompts per distribution. The authors do test HumanEval and UltraChat in the API audit, which helps, but the core kernel comparison in Section 4 is mostly on Wikipedia continuation. Since the paper argues for user-customized auditing, it would be useful to see more diversity in the simulation study itself: dialogue, summarization, instruction following, safety-sensitive prompts, or prompts with stronger semantic constraints. The appendix result in Figure 8 suggests power improves with more prompts, which is encouraging, but it also raises the question of how prompt selection affects detectability. Are there prompt distributions under which the Hamming kernel performs poorly even for meaningful distortions?

Another issue is the baseline selection. The paper compares against several classical tests, but some stronger modern baselines seem absent. For example, one could imagine embedding-based two-sample tests using sentence embeddings, hidden-state features from a reference model, or n-gram feature maps beyond exact positionwise matches. Even within kernel methods, there are many string kernels between one-hot and Hamming. The all-substrings kernel is included but is computationally expensive and perhaps not tuned for this setting. Since the paper’s main methodological claim is that a simple Hamming kernel is especially effective, it would be useful to compare against at least one semantic or representation-based baseline. Otherwise, it is hard to know whether the observed gains are due to MMD per se, the low-sample regime, or simply the weakness of the chosen alternatives.

The goodness-of-fit comparison in Appendix C.3 is interesting but underdeveloped. The finding that approximate goodness-of-fit tests can underperform two-sample tests despite privileged probability access is surprising and potentially important. However, because this section is relegated to the appendix and uses approximations that introduce bias, it currently reads more like an exploratory aside than a solid conclusion. I would either downplay it further or expand it with clearer explanation and perhaps a more principled approximation scheme.

I appreciated the qualitative examples, but some of them also highlight a subtle issue: the test may detect stylistic or entropy differences that are not necessarily harmful, while missing semantically important but distributionally subtle changes. Figure 4 on page 9 shows only moderate correlation between MMD and HumanEval accuracy differences. The authors correctly note that there are multiple ways to be wrong, and MMD captures more than accuracy. Still, from a user perspective, it matters whether a detected difference is consequential. The paper would benefit from a more explicit discussion of how users should interpret a rejection. Does a large Hamming-MMD imply degraded utility, or just different phrasing? The effect-size analysis helps, but some calibration to downstream impact would strengthen the practical story.

On clarity, the paper is generally well written. The exposition of MMD is concise and accessible, and the figures are informative. I especially liked Figure 3 right, which clusters models by estimated pairwise distances, and the appendix heatmaps comparing providers. One minor issue is that some notation and estimator definitions could be tightened. For example, Equation 4 uses equal sample sizes only, with unequal sizes deferred to the appendix; given the practical setting, unequal sizes seem common enough to deserve at least a brief main-text formula. Also, the distinction between token-space and character-space testing is important and should perhaps be emphasized earlier, since it materially affects power, as seen in Table 8.

I also want to note the conflict-of-interest disclosure is appropriate and appreciated, especially given that one author is affiliated with a provider evaluated in the paper. The paper’s release of code and data is another strong positive for reproducibility.

In terms of significance, I think this work could have substantial impact. Auditing black-box LLM APIs is a real need, and the paper offers a concrete, low-cost tool that many practitioners could use. Even if the Hamming-MMD test is not a universal solution, the framing itself is valuable and likely to stimulate follow-up work on stronger tests, better kernels, and broader modalities. The paper’s empirical finding that many commercial endpoints differ from released weights is also likely to attract attention.

My main suggestions for improvement are as follows. First, sharpen the claims around what is and is not being tested. The current method is best described as a powerful practical detector for many common distortions, not a definitive equality test for full sequence distributions. Second, provide a more rigorous treatment of the endpoint-level decision rule in Section 5, including sensitivity analyses for the repeated-test aggregation threshold and perhaps confidence intervals. Third, expand discussion of confounders in the API audit, especially chat templates, system prompts, safety layers, and temporal drift during collection. Fourth, add at least one stronger baseline based on semantic or learned representations, or justify more clearly why such baselines are out of scope. Fifth, broaden the simulation study or at least discuss more explicitly how prompt distribution choice affects power and user-facing applicability.

To summarize my assessment: this is a strong and timely paper with a compelling problem formulation, useful methodology, and impactful empirical findings. Its main weakness is that the chosen test statistic is not fully aligned with the breadth of the “model equality” framing, and some of the audit conclusions rely on somewhat ad hoc aggregation choices and potentially confounded endpoint comparisons. Still, I think the paper makes a meaningful contribution and is close to publishable quality. With clearer positioning and some additional robustness analysis, it would be substantially stronger.

My recommendation is positive but not without reservations.

This is a strong, timely, and well-executed paper on an increasingly important problem: how users can audit black-box LLM APIs to determine whether they are actually serving the model distribution they claim to serve, or whether that distribution has changed due to quantization, watermarking, finetuning, implementation differences, or silent updates. The paper’s central contribution is to formalize this as a two-sample hypothesis testing problem, “Model Equality Testing,” and to show that a simple MMD-based test with an appropriate string kernel is surprisingly effective in practice. The work is both conceptually clean and practically consequential. It addresses a real gap in the current LLM ecosystem, where users often rely on third-party inference providers without any principled way to verify distributional faithfulness or temporal stability.

The framing is excellent. The paper clearly motivates two concrete auditing questions: whether an API has modified a reference model’s distribution, and whether an API has drifted over time. Casting both under a unified statistical testing lens is elegant and useful. I especially appreciated that the authors focus on the sampling setting rather than only greedy decoding or benchmark accuracy. This is a major strength: many practical applications depend on the full output distribution, not just top-1 behavior, and the paper makes a convincing case that existing benchmark-based audits are too narrow for this purpose. The problem formulation in Section 2 is crisp, and the distinction between sample access and log-probability access is handled thoughtfully.

Methodologically, the paper is simple in the best sense. The use of MMD is natural, but the key insight is that kernel choice determines both semantics and power. The comparison between the one-hot kernel, all-substrings kernel, and the proposed Hamming-style string kernel is very informative. The Hamming kernel is computationally cheap, interpretable, and empirically powerful, even though it is only a pseudometric rather than a fully characteristic metric. I found this tradeoff well justified. The paper does not oversell universality; instead, it argues persuasively that in the small-sample regime, a non-universal but better-biased feature map can be much more useful than a theoretically stronger but practically weak alternative. This is exactly the kind of pragmatic statistical design that often matters in real ML systems work.

The empirical evaluation is a major strength. The simulation suite is broad and well chosen: quantization, watermarking, finetuning, and model substitution are all realistic distortions. The headline result that the Hamming MMD test achieves median power of 77.4% with roughly 10 samples per prompt is impressive, especially given the high-dimensionality of the completion space. The plots on pages 6–7 are particularly compelling: the sample complexity comparison in Figure 2, the robustness to longer completions, and the finetuning detection results all support the paper’s claims well. I also appreciated the analysis of pairwise distances between models in Figure 3 on page 7. The observation that models cluster more by family than by size is interesting in its own right and shows that the framework is useful not only for hypothesis testing but also for exploratory model comparison.

The real-world audit of commercial Llama endpoints is the paper’s most impactful component. Applying the method to 31 endpoints across nine providers and four Llama variants makes the work much more than a methodological exercise. The finding that 11 of 31 endpoints differ from Meta’s released reference distributions is important and likely to attract substantial attention. The tables and figures in Section 5 are clear and informative. In particular, Table 1 on page 9 gives a concise summary of which providers fail under which tasks, while Figure 4 adds useful effect-size context by showing that some deviations are as large as swapping in an entirely different model family. This is a striking result. The qualitative examples in Box 2 and Appendix D also help ground the statistical findings in observable behavioral differences.

Another notable strength is the paper’s attention to practical usability. The authors release code, a Python package, and a large dataset of 1.1M completions. This substantially increases the paper’s value to the community. The appendices are also unusually thorough. I found the discussion of p-value estimation, permutation testing, composite nulls, asymmetric sampling costs, and approximate goodness-of-fit comparisons to be careful and useful. The paper does a good job of anticipating likely reviewer questions and addressing them empirically.

I also want to highlight the paper’s clarity. The writing is polished, the motivation is easy to follow, and the figures are generally strong. The visual summary in Figure 1 on page 2 is effective, and the progression from formalization to simulations to deployment is well structured. The paper is accessible to both ML systems and statistics audiences without sacrificing rigor.

There are a few limitations, but they are relatively minor and mostly point to future work rather than undermining the current contribution. First, the strongest empirical results depend on a particular kernel choice and prompt distribution design. While the authors do test across multiple prompt sets and tasks, the method’s sensitivity to prompt selection remains important in practice. Figure 8 in the appendix suggests that power improves with more prompts, which is useful, but it would be helpful to have a bit more guidance in the main text on how an end user should choose prompts for a custom audit and how robust conclusions are to prompt mismatch. That said, the paper already goes farther than most prior work in evaluating prompt variation.

Second, the Hamming kernel’s non-injectivity is acknowledged, but the practical implications could be discussed a bit more explicitly in the main paper rather than mostly in Appendix A. In principle, there are distribution shifts that this kernel will miss. The empirical evidence suggests this is not a serious issue for the distortions studied here, but a short discussion of plausible failure modes would strengthen the presentation. Relatedly, the weak performance against fp16 in some settings is interesting and deserves a slightly more developed interpretation. The paper notes that fp16/fp32 differences may not be well captured by Hamming distance; expanding on what kinds of shifts are “orthogonal” to this kernel would be valuable.

Third, the API audit methodology necessarily faces confounds from provider-side prompt templating, decoding implementation details, caching, and time-varying backend changes. The authors are careful about matching chat templates and documenting collection dates in the appendix, which I appreciated. Still, because the paper’s conclusions are about endpoint distributions rather than necessarily intentional provider modifications, the wording should remain precise throughout. In most places it is, but a few claims could perhaps more consistently emphasize that the test detects distributional inequality, not its cause. This is not a flaw in the method, just an interpretational nuance.

Fourth, the composite null in Section 5 is sensible but somewhat conservative, and the decision to threshold average rejection rate over ten samples at 0.5 is pragmatic rather than fully formal. I understand why this was done to reduce variance and cost, and the appendix provides supporting detail, but a bit more statistical justification for this aggregation rule would improve the end-to-end audit story. Even so, the main conclusions appear robust, especially given the large effect sizes for several flagged endpoints.

A smaller presentation issue is that some appendix examples and tables are dense, and a few qualitative samples are more anecdotal than diagnostic. This is not a major concern, since the core quantitative evidence is strong, but the paper could perhaps streamline a few appendix elements or better connect them to the main claims.

Overall, I found this paper highly compelling. It identifies an important and underexplored problem, proposes a principled and practical solution, validates it extensively, and demonstrates real-world impact through a substantial audit of commercial APIs. The combination of statistical formalization, empirical depth, and practical relevance is excellent. This feels like exactly the kind of work that can shape how the community thinks about auditing and reproducibility for black-box LLM services.

My recommendation is to accept. The paper is novel, technically sound, empirically strong, and broadly useful. It should be of interest to researchers in LLM evaluation, trustworthy ML, ML systems, and applied statistics, and I expect it to stimulate follow-up work on stronger tests, adaptive prompt selection, and auditing beyond text generation.

This paper studies reward overoptimization in RLHF and proposes a theoretically motivated objective that leads to a practical algorithm, Regularized Preference Optimization (RPO), which augments DPO with an imitation/SFT term. The central claim is appealing and important: the SFT loss can be interpreted as an implicit adversarial regularizer that mitigates overoptimization caused by reward uncertainty and distribution shift. The paper combines a maximin formulation, an equivalence argument to a minimax/practical objective, finite-sample guarantees under a partial coverage condition, and empirical results on LLM alignment benchmarks. Overall, I found the paper interesting, timely, and potentially impactful. The main conceptual message—that a simple SFT term can be justified as a principled regularizer against overoptimization—is valuable. At the same time, there are several places where the theory-to-practice bridge is not yet fully convincing, some assumptions and derivations need clarification, and the empirical evidence, while promising, is still somewhat limited relative to the strength of the claims.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the unifying perspective it offers. The formulation in Sections 3 and 4 is elegant: starting from a pessimistic/adversarial reward estimation objective and arriving at a practical loss that is simply “DPO + SFT” is a neat result. The intuition is well conveyed, especially through Figure 1 on page 3, which illustrates how DPO can assign probability mass to undesirable but weakly constrained responses, while RPO’s extra log-likelihood term pushes mass back toward desirable/chosen responses. This is a compelling story, and the paper does a good job motivating why standard KL regularization to the reference model may be insufficient: as argued in Section 4, the DPO temperature/scaling parameter mainly rescales gradients per example, whereas the added imitation term can alter the gradient direction. That distinction is useful and, if made fully rigorous, could be an important contribution.

The theoretical contribution is also nontrivial. The paper proposes a maximin objective over policies and reward models in a general function approximation setting, rather than restricting to linear rewards. The finite-sample guarantee in Theorem 5.3 gives a suboptimality bound scaling roughly as a coverage-dependent term times 1/sqrt(N), plus a KL-to-reference term. This is a meaningful result in the offline RLHF setting, where partial coverage is the right lens. I also appreciate that the paper explicitly discusses the role of the baseline policy and ties it to identifiability under Bradley-Terry preferences. The equivalence result in Section 5.2, connecting the maximin objective to the minimax objective and then to the practical RPO loss, is the key theoretical bridge that makes the paper more than just “another DPO variant with SFT.”

That said, I have several concerns about the theory. First, the practical algorithm optimizes over a parameterized policy class, but the formal guarantees are stated for the idealized optimization problems over policy/reward classes, not for the actual nonconvex neural optimization used in experiments. This gap is common, but here it matters because the paper’s main selling point is the theory-to-practice equivalence. Theorem 5.6 shows that if one solves the minimax problem exactly, then the induced policy solves the maximin problem. But the practical RPO implementation in Algorithm 2 does not solve the minimax problem over reward models; it directly optimizes a parameterized policy objective. The paper informally motivates this via the reward-policy reparameterization, but the exact conditions under which the parameterized policy class corresponds to the image of the reward class are not spelled out. In practice, the optimization landscape and parameterization constraints may break the equivalence. The paper should be much more explicit about what is actually guaranteed for the implemented algorithm versus the idealized objective.

Second, Assumption 5.5 is doing substantial work and feels under-discussed. The “convex-like” condition on the reward class is fairly abstract, and while the paper notes that convex reward classes satisfy it, the practical relevance to neural reward classes or implicit policy parameterizations is unclear. Since the paper emphasizes general function approximation, it would help to characterize concrete nontrivial classes where the assumption holds and where the equivalence theorem is meaningful. As written, the result is mathematically valid but may be narrower in applicability than the presentation suggests.

Third, there is some notational and conceptual slippage around the baseline policy. In Section 3, the baseline is introduced as necessary because Bradley-Terry only identifies reward differences. In theory, this baseline should be chosen to satisfy coverage properties. In practice, the paper uses chosen responses from the preference dataset, which is reasonable and supported by Remark 5.4 and Appendix A. However, the practical objective in Equation (4.5) becomes an expectation over prompts from d0 and actions from pi_base. In implementation, this seems to reduce to standard SFT on chosen responses from the dataset, but the exact correspondence between the theoretical expectation and the empirical loss is not fully spelled out. Since this baseline choice is central to the method, the paper should clarify whether the practical estimator is unbiased for the theoretical term, and how prompt-distribution mismatch is handled.

Fourth, the generalization argument in Section 5.3 is fairly weak relative to the empirical claims. Corollary 5.8 assumes bounded density ratio between the new prompt distribution and the training prompt distribution. The paper then uses PCA plots of prompt embeddings on page 12 to argue that this “approximately holds” for MT-Bench and AlpacaEval. This is not a convincing validation of a density-ratio assumption. PCA overlap in two dimensions is at best a rough visualization and does not establish coverage or bounded density ratio in the original space. I would strongly recommend toning down the theoretical justification for benchmark generalization, or replacing it with a more careful empirical analysis of prompt-distribution similarity.

On the empirical side, the results are encouraging but not yet fully persuasive. The paper evaluates on two 7B model families, beta and gemma, using training setups modeled after Zephyr variants. The reported gains over DPO are consistent but modest on standard benchmarks. For example, Table 2 on page 14 shows MT-Bench improvements from 7.278 to 7.381 for beta and from 7.688 to 7.916 for gemma, and AlpacaEval 2.0 gains that are similarly positive but not dramatic. These are good signs, but given the variability of LLM evaluation pipelines, especially with GPT-4-based judging, it would be important to report variance across seeds or repeated runs. The paper uses a single seed (42) according to Table 3 on page 29. Without multiple runs, it is hard to know whether the gains are robust.

Relatedly, the in-distribution evaluation on 150 GPT-4-annotated examples is too small to support strong conclusions. Table 1 on page 14 reports pairwise win rates, but no confidence intervals or significance tests are provided. Since the margins over DPO are not huge, statistical uncertainty matters. The same issue applies to the benchmark comparisons. I would like to see either bootstrap confidence intervals over prompts or repeated training/evaluation runs.

A more substantive empirical concern is that the paper does not sufficiently disentangle whether the gains come from the specific adversarial-regularization interpretation or simply from adding extra supervised signal. In other words, is RPO better because the chosen-response SFT term is theoretically special, or because any auxiliary likelihood regularizer would help stabilize DPO? The paper argues for the former, but the experiments do not test it. Stronger ablations are needed: varying the baseline distribution, comparing chosen-response SFT versus reference-model imitation versus rejected-response penalties, and matching total optimization budget/token exposure. Since the core claim is that “your SFT loss is implicitly an adversarial regularizer,” the paper should empirically validate that the particular SFT term predicted by the theory matters.

The comparison set is also somewhat narrow. The related work section acknowledges methods such as ORPO, DPO-positive/Smaug, and other preference optimization variants that incorporate SFT-like or monolithic regularization. Yet the experiments compare primarily against vanilla DPO and the released Zephyr models. Since some prior methods already combine preference optimization with supervised terms, the novelty claim would be much stronger if the paper compared directly against those baselines. Otherwise, it is difficult to assess whether the contribution is mainly theoretical reinterpretation or whether RPO is empirically superior to the closest alternatives.

There are also a few technical presentation issues that should be fixed. In Section 5.2, Equation (5.2) appears to define phi using pi_ref in the expectation over a0, whereas earlier sections use pi_base; this looks like either a typo or an inconsistency and should be corrected. On page 9, the notation for r_theta is written as beta · log(pi_theta(a|x))/log(pi_ref(a|x)), which seems dimensionally wrong; presumably it should be beta times the log-ratio, i.e., beta (log pi_theta(a|x) - log pi_ref(a|x)). There are several minor typographical issues throughout, but this one affects the mathematical meaning. I also noticed some inconsistencies in table labels in Appendix E.3 on page 30, where the headers for gemma tables still say “RPO (beta)” / “Ref. (beta)” / “DPO (beta).” These are small but should be cleaned up.

Another point that deserves more discussion is the choice of hyperparameter eta. In practice, eta is selected on a held-out test split of the training dataset according to Section 6 and Appendix E.1. Since eta controls the strength of the imitation regularizer, the method’s effectiveness may depend heavily on tuning. The paper should provide a sensitivity analysis over eta and beta, ideally showing whether RPO is robust across a reasonable range. This is especially important because one of the claimed advantages is practical simplicity. If the gains require careful tuning of eta per setup, that should be stated clearly.

I did appreciate the additional experiments in Appendix F on GSM8K, ARC, and MBPP. These results suggest that the regularizer does not obviously hurt reasoning/coding performance and may even help slightly. Still, these experiments use a modified variant of RPO implemented in a different codebase with a token-normalized SFT term and different beta, which makes them less directly comparable to the main results. They are useful as supplementary evidence but should not be overinterpreted.

In terms of significance, I think the paper has real promise. The idea that a simple SFT term can emerge from a pessimistic/adversarial treatment of reward uncertainty is conceptually strong and likely to interest both the RLHF theory and practice communities. The paper is also commendable for trying to connect offline RLHF theory to implementation-friendly objectives, which many theoretical works fail to do. If the authors can tighten the theory/practice correspondence, strengthen the empirical validation with better ablations and stronger baselines, and clean up the presentation, this could become a strong contribution.

My main suggestions for improvement are as follows. First, clearly separate the guarantees for the idealized maximin/minimax objectives from what is actually optimized in neural RPO, and state the additional assumptions needed for the practical parameterized policy version. Second, expand the discussion of Assumption 5.5 and give concrete examples of reward classes where it holds in a meaningful way. Third, add ablations on the baseline distribution and the form of the SFT regularizer to test the central theoretical claim. Fourth, compare against the closest practical baselines that also mix preference optimization with supervised terms. Fifth, report uncertainty estimates and, ideally, multiple seeds. Sixth, fix the notation/typos and improve consistency in the appendices.

Overall, my assessment is positive but somewhat tempered. The paper contains a compelling idea, a nice theoretical framing, and promising empirical evidence, but it currently overstates the strength of the theory-to-practice bridge and under-supports some of its empirical claims. With revisions, I could see this being a valuable paper. In its current form, I would lean borderline accept at a venue that values conceptual novelty and theory-practice integration, but I think it still needs stronger empirical rigor and sharper exposition to be fully convincing.

This paper studies a central and timely problem in RLHF: overoptimization against an imperfect reward model or preference objective. The main claim is both conceptually appealing and practically relevant: adding an SFT-style imitation term to preference optimization can be understood as an implicit adversarial regularizer, and this yields both provable robustness benefits and a simple practical algorithm, RPO, that augments DPO with an SFT loss. Overall, I found the paper strong. It addresses an important failure mode in alignment, proposes a clean theoretical formulation, derives a practical objective with a surprisingly simple implementation, and supports the claims with both theory and experiments on real LLM alignment setups. The paper is ambitious in scope, spanning offline RLHF theory under general function approximation, minimax/maximin equivalence, and empirical validation on multiple benchmarks. In my view, this is a meaningful contribution.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the bridge it builds between theory and practice. The theoretical starting point in Section 3 is a maximin objective where the policy is optimized against an adversarial reward model that minimizes a combination of MLE loss and a reward penalty term. This is a principled way to encode pessimism under reward uncertainty and distribution shift. The practical payoff is especially elegant: through the KL-regularized optimal policy characterization and the minimax reformulation in Section 4, the authors derive an implementation-friendly objective that is simply preference optimization plus imitation loss. This is a compelling result because it gives a theoretical explanation for a very practical recipe that practitioners can adopt immediately. The title claim that “your SFT loss is implicitly an adversarial regularizer” is therefore not just rhetorical; the paper does a good job substantiating it mathematically.

I also appreciated the clarity of the motivating intuition. Figure 1 on page 3 is effective: the left panel illustrates the mismatch between desired and undesired responses under uncertainty, the middle panel shows the degradation of log-probability on chosen responses during DPO training, and the right panel gives a simple three-action example where DPO can place mass on an uncovered bad action while RPO avoids it. This figure does real explanatory work and helps connect the abstract pessimism argument to concrete overoptimization behavior. The discussion in Appendix A further clarifies why monitoring chosen-response probability can be informative about reward overoptimization.

From a theoretical standpoint, the paper is quite substantial. The sample complexity result in Theorem 5.3 is meaningful: under a partial coverage condition and finite covering number assumptions on the reward class, the algorithm achieves an approximately O(1/sqrt(N)) suboptimality gap against any comparator policy whose induced distribution is sufficiently covered. I particularly liked that the analysis is framed under general function approximation rather than only linear models, which broadens the conceptual relevance. The partial coverage assumption in Assumption 5.2 is also well motivated and aligns with the offline RL literature. The equivalence result in Section 5.2 is another highlight. Showing that the minimax-derived practical policy also solves the original maximin objective is important for legitimizing the practical algorithm rather than presenting it as merely heuristic.

The empirical section is also solid and, importantly, aligned with the paper’s central claims. The experiments use two realistic model/data pipelines, Zephyr-7b-beta with UltraFeedback and Zephyr-7b-gemma with Argilla-DPO-Mix-7K, which helps demonstrate that the method is not tied to a single reference model or dataset. The training curves on pages 3 and 14 support the claim that RPO alleviates the drop in log-probability on chosen responses seen with DPO. The in-distribution pairwise GPT-4 evaluations in Table 1 show consistent gains over DPO for both series. The benchmark results in Table 2 are also encouraging: RPO improves over DPO on MT-Bench and AlpacaEval 2.0 for both beta and gemma variants, and the appendix extends this to GSM8K, ARC, and MBPP. The practical message is attractive: a simple plug-in regularizer appears to improve alignment quality without requiring extra preference data or a more complex RL pipeline.

That said, there are several points where the paper could be strengthened further.

First, while the theory-to-practice derivation is elegant, the exact relationship between the theoretical algorithm and the implemented RPO objective still feels somewhat idealized. The theory optimizes over a reward class and policy class with exact minimax/maximin structure, whereas the practical implementation uses parameterized LLMs trained by gradient descent on a surrogate objective. This gap is unavoidable to some extent, but the paper could be more explicit about which parts of the guarantee survive approximation, optimization error, and finite-capacity parameterization. Corollary 5.7 states suboptimality for minimax-based algorithms, but the actual neural optimization dynamics of Algorithm 2 are not analyzed. As written, the theory justifies the objective form more than the trained neural solution. This is still valuable, but the distinction should be stated more plainly.

Second, the assumptions behind the minimax equivalence deserve a bit more discussion. Assumption 5.5 requires compactness and a convex-like property of the reward class. The paper notes that convex reward classes satisfy this, but in realistic LLM settings the implicit reward classes induced by neural parameterizations are highly nonconvex. Since the practical significance of Theorem 5.6 is central, it would help to clarify whether the theorem should be interpreted mainly as a conceptual justification rather than a literal guarantee for neural training. I do not view this as a fatal issue, but the current presentation may overstate how directly the formal equivalence transfers to modern deep learning practice.

Third, the empirical evaluation, while promising, is somewhat narrow relative to the breadth of the claims. The paper argues that RPO mitigates overoptimization due to uncertainty and distribution shift, but the experiments mostly compare against vanilla DPO and released DPO-trained models. Since the related work section explicitly mentions methods such as ORPO, Smaug/DPO-positive, reward ensembles, constrained RLHF, and other regularized preference optimization variants, stronger baselines would make the empirical case more convincing. In particular, because some prior methods also add SFT-like or positive-example regularization, it would be useful to compare directly against those approaches rather than only DPO. This is especially important because the novelty claim is partly theoretical understanding, but the practical algorithmic form may overlap with existing heuristics.

Fourth, the evaluation methodology relies heavily on GPT-4-as-judge. This is standard practice, and the authors do take some care with prompt design and position randomization in Appendix E.2, but it remains a limitation. Human evaluation, even on a modest subset, would strengthen the alignment claims considerably. At minimum, reporting confidence intervals or bootstrap uncertainty for the pairwise win rates and benchmark scores would help assess robustness. The current tables report point estimates only, and some gains, while consistent, are not very large.

Fifth, the choice of the baseline policy for the imitation term is important both theoretically and practically, but the empirical exploration of this design choice is limited. The theory allows flexibility, and the paper mentions options such as preferred responses or initial model responses. In experiments, the chosen responses are used. An ablation comparing different baseline distributions would be very informative, especially because the central claim is that the SFT loss acts as an adversarial regularizer when the baseline is suitably covered by data. It would also help clarify whether the gains come specifically from imitating chosen responses or more generally from adding any anchor toward in-distribution behavior.

Sixth, I would have liked more ablations on the regularization strength and interaction with beta. The paper argues in Section 4 that beta in DPO mainly rescales gradients while eta changes gradient direction through the imitation term. This is an interesting claim, but the empirical section only briefly states that eta was selected as 0.005. A sweep over eta, and perhaps a joint eta/beta sensitivity analysis, would make the practical guidance much stronger. Similarly, since the paper emphasizes overoptimization during training, it would be useful to show how performance evolves over epochs for DPO versus RPO, not just the chosen-response log-probability.

There are also a few presentation and technical issues that should be cleaned up. In Section 5.2, the definition of phi in equation (5.2) appears to use pi_ref in the expectation over a0, whereas earlier sections define the baseline policy more generally as pi_base; this may be a typo or notational inconsistency and should be corrected. There are a handful of minor grammatical issues and notation slips throughout, but none are serious. I also think the paper could do a better job distinguishing what is formally proved from what is empirically suggested. For example, the PCA plots on page 12 are used to support the coverage intuition for benchmark prompts, but this is only a rough visualization and should not be read as evidence that the density ratio assumption actually holds.

Despite these concerns, my overall assessment is positive. The paper tackles an important problem, offers a genuinely insightful theoretical perspective, and derives a practical algorithm that is simple enough to matter. The conceptual contribution is stronger than a typical “add one more regularizer” paper because it explains why the regularizer should help and ties it to adversarial pessimism under uncertainty. The empirical results, while not exhaustive, are consistent with the theory and demonstrate practical promise on realistic LLM alignment pipelines. I expect this work to be of interest to both the RLHF theory community and practitioners working on preference optimization.

The most valuable revisions would be to add stronger empirical baselines, include ablations over the baseline policy and eta, report uncertainty estimates, and clarify the scope of the theoretical guarantees relative to neural optimization. But even in its current form, I think the paper makes a worthwhile contribution.

In summary, this is a strong paper with a clear idea, elegant derivation, meaningful theory, and encouraging experiments. Its central message—that SFT-style imitation can be understood as a principled adversarial regularizer against overoptimization in RLHF—is novel, useful, and likely to influence future work. I would lean toward acceptance.

This paper studies motion forecasting under a more realistic continuous-driving setting, arguing that standard benchmarks and methods treat each scene independently even though real autonomous driving systems repeatedly forecast over temporally adjacent scenes. To address this mismatch, the authors propose RealMotion, which combines a data reorganization strategy that converts benchmark scenes into short continuous sub-scene sequences, a scene context stream that propagates historical scene information forward, and an agent trajectory stream that relays past predictions through a trajectory memory bank. Experiments on Argoverse 1 and 2 suggest improved forecasting accuracy over prior methods, with favorable latency and parameter count.

Overall, I find the paper interesting and timely. The central motivation is compelling: most motion forecasting work indeed assumes isolated samples, whereas deployment is inherently streaming. I also appreciate that the paper does not merely add temporal recurrence to a model, but explicitly reframes the task and benchmark usage to better reflect continuous inference. The empirical results are strong, especially on Argoverse 2, and the method appears relatively lightweight. At the same time, there are several conceptual and experimental issues that should be clarified before I would fully trust the claims. In particular, the proposed “continuous” setting is synthesized from originally independent benchmark scenes, and the paper currently does not fully disentangle gains from extra supervision/data augmentation versus gains from true temporal state propagation. There are also some ambiguities in the methodology and fairness of comparisons.

The main strength of the paper is the problem formulation. The introduction and Figure 1 on page 2 clearly articulate the gap between one-shot forecasting and repeated online forecasting. This is a meaningful perspective shift, and one that is underexplored in the literature. The example in Figure 1(c), where historical context may reveal an agent that is currently invisible, is intuitive and helps motivate why temporal continuity could matter beyond simply having a longer history window. This framing alone makes the paper relevant to the community.

A second strength is that the method is conceptually simple and modular. The architecture in Figure 3 on page 4 is easy to follow: an encoder-decoder backbone is augmented with two temporal streams, one operating on scene features and one on predicted trajectories. The scene context stream uses cross-attention from current features to aligned historical features, while the trajectory stream uses a memory bank of prior predicted trajectories and mode features to refine current predictions. This decomposition is sensible: scene context and trajectory continuity are distinct sources of temporal information, and the ablations in Table 4 on page 8 suggest both contribute.

A third strength is the empirical performance. On the Argoverse 2 test leaderboard in Table 1 on page 6, RealMotion improves over QCNet on minFDE1 and minADE1 and is competitive or best on most other metrics. The multi-agent results in Table 3 on page 7 are also strong. The efficiency analysis in Table 6 on page 9 is another positive aspect: the model is much smaller than QCNet and appears to retain practical online latency. If these numbers are measured fairly, this is a meaningful contribution.

That said, my biggest concern is whether the paper cleanly demonstrates improvement due to continuous forecasting rather than due to altered training data and evaluation protocol. The data reorganization strategy on page 3 is central: each benchmark scene is split into multiple sub-scenes by choosing split points along the historical trajectory and constructing shorter segments with associated local context. This effectively creates multiple training/evaluation instances from one original scene. Table 4 shows that simply using “Con. Data” already improves performance noticeably over the independent baseline. This raises an important question: how much of the gain comes from a better temporal model, and how much comes from additional supervision, denser sampling of the same scene, or a curriculum-like effect? The paper partially acknowledges this by including RealMotion-I and the “Con. Data” ablation, but the current presentation still overstates the architectural contribution unless this issue is more carefully controlled.

Relatedly, the comparison to prior work may not be fully apples-to-apples. RealMotion is evaluated after reorganizing the data into continuous sub-scenes, whereas prior methods in Tables 1–3 were trained in their original settings. The appendix does include one useful generality experiment where QCNet benefits from the reorganized data (Table 9 on page 13), which supports the claim that the data structure itself is helpful. However, this also weakens the attribution of gains specifically to RealMotion. A stronger and fairer comparison would retrain stronger baselines under the same reorganized continuous setting, ideally including at least one recurrent or memory-based baseline and one simple “longer-history” baseline. Without this, it is difficult to know whether the proposed streams are necessary, or whether much of the gain would arise from exposing any strong model to the reorganized data.

A second major concern is the realism of the “continuous driving” benchmark construction. The paper claims to narrow the gap to real-world applications, but the constructed sequences are still retrospective slices from a single benchmark sample rather than true online streams across long horizons. The sub-scenes share the same original future trajectory annotations and are generated by splitting the historical portion at fixed points. This is useful, but it is not equivalent to deployment-time streaming where perception noise, map changes, agent entrance/exit, and long-term state accumulation matter. The limitation section on page 10 briefly notes that existing datasets provide limited historical information, but the paper should be more explicit that this is a proxy setting rather than a true continuous benchmark. As written, some claims sound stronger than the evidence supports.

A third concern is possible information leakage or at least ambiguity in how the reorganized samples are formed. On page 3, the paper says it “retrospectively examine[s] each independent scene by evenly splitting agent trajectories into shorter segments and sampling local map elements,” and that trajectory segments are generated by extending from split points “both into the past and the future.” This is reasonable if only the appropriate future after each split point is used as target, but the description is not precise enough to rule out subtle leakage in preprocessing or normalization. Since all states are normalized relative to the current position of the agent of interest, and because multiple sub-scenes come from the same original trajectory, the exact train/val/test handling matters. The paper should explicitly state that no future information beyond each split point is used in constructing inputs or selecting context, and ideally provide pseudocode for the reorganization pipeline.

Methodologically, the scene context stream is plausible but somewhat under-justified. Equation (2) on page 5 uses map-map cross-attention and agent-scene cross-attention after alignment with MLN. However, it is not obvious why map features should only attend to historical map features while agent features attend to the full historical scene. Since the map is static in Argoverse, the benefit of temporal map propagation is unclear unless the local crop changes over time and historical map tokens recover currently out-of-view lanes. If that is the intended effect, the paper should say so explicitly. Otherwise, this component may be doing little more than expanding the spatial map context through time. A more detailed analysis of what information is actually transferred in the scene stream would strengthen the paper.

The agent trajectory stream is interesting, but it also raises questions. The memory bank stores predicted trajectories and mode features, not ground-truth trajectories. This is realistic for online inference, but it introduces the possibility of error accumulation. The paper argues that refinement is more effective than direct decoding from memory, which is sensible, yet there is no explicit analysis of drift over long sequences. Because the benchmark sequences are only three sub-scenes long in the main Argoverse 2 setup, the method may not be tested under sufficiently long horizons to reveal compounding errors. A longer unrolled evaluation, even if only on validation data, would be valuable. Similarly, the choice not to filter memory trajectories “to ensure multimodality and diversity” may also preserve poor modes; some discussion or ablation on memory size and quality control would help.

The experimental section is generally solid, but several details need clarification. First, the paper reports both “offline” and “online” latency in Table 6 on page 9, but the definition is somewhat confusing. For RealMotion, offline latency is roughly three times online latency because the reorganized dataset has three segments and only the final prediction is used for evaluation. This makes sense operationally, but it also means the reported online latency is not directly comparable to standard benchmark inference, where one prediction per sample is required. The paper should clearly separate deployment-time amortized latency from benchmark-time per-sample latency and avoid implying direct equivalence. Second, the latency comparison to HPTR and QCNet would be more convincing if all methods were remeasured under the same codebase assumptions, preprocessing pipeline, and hardware/software stack.

I also found the Argoverse 1 results less convincing than the Argoverse 2 results. In Table 2 on page 7, RealMotion achieves the best minADE6 but not the best minFDE6, where HPNet remains stronger. Since the paper’s main claim is state-of-the-art performance, it should be phrased more carefully across datasets and metrics. The current wording occasionally overgeneralizes from selected metrics. Likewise, in Table 1, RealMotion is best on several metrics but not all; “state-of-the-art” is fair overall on Argoverse 2 test, but the narrative should acknowledge where it is merely competitive.

The ablation studies are useful, especially Tables 4, 5, and 7 on pages 8–10. I appreciated that the authors separately analyze the contributions of continuous data, the scene context stream, the agent trajectory stream, alignment modules, trajectory embedding, split points, gradient steps, and cross-attention depth. However, some of these ablations still leave open questions. For example, Table 5(b) varies split points and gradient steps jointly with the reorganized setting, but there is no comparison to simply increasing the historical observation window in the baseline model. Since the core claim is that sequential propagation adds value beyond one-shot forecasting, a strong control would be to give RealMotion-I access to the same total temporal span, perhaps by concatenating more history or using a larger receptive field. If that baseline closes much of the gap, the novelty claim would need to be moderated.

The qualitative results are a nice addition. Figure 4 on page 9 and Figures 6–7 in the appendix show progressive refinement over steps, and the comparison to RealMotion-I is visually persuasive in several cases. The failure cases on page 14 are also appreciated; they suggest the model still struggles with rare maneuvers such as turning through complex intersections and parking-like subjective behavior. That said, the qualitative evidence would be stronger if the paper included examples where the scene context stream specifically helps due to temporarily occluded or out-of-view agents, since this is one of the motivating examples in Figure 1(c). Right now, the qualitative section mostly shows generic refinement rather than uniquely continuous-context reasoning.

There are also some presentation issues. The writing is mostly understandable, but there are grammatical errors and occasional imprecision. For example, the paper sometimes says “forecast a singular trajectory” where “single trajectory” would be clearer, and there are several awkward phrasings throughout Sections 3 and 4. Some notation is also introduced too tersely. In Equation (3), the indexing for the trajectory origin y_ori_i = y_i[Δt · q] is not fully explained, especially when Δt varies across memory entries. The memory bank size n is never specified in the main text. The exact number of modes, decoder structure, and whether the auxiliary trajectory for other agents is used at inference are also not fully clear. These are fixable, but the paper would benefit from a careful revision for clarity and reproducibility.

In terms of novelty relative to prior work, I view the contribution as moderate but meaningful. The idea of streaming or temporal forecasting is not entirely new, as the paper cites prior work on streaming motion forecasting, and memory-based temporal refinement has analogues in adjacent tasks. However, the combination of benchmark reorganization, scene-level temporal context propagation, and trajectory-memory refinement for motion forecasting is reasonably novel. The strongest novelty is arguably the reframing of the task and the practical emphasis on continuous inference, rather than any single architectural block.

To strengthen the paper, I would recommend the following concrete additions. First, include stronger controlled baselines under the same reorganized data setting, ideally QCNet and one lightweight model retrained on continuous sub-scenes, plus a simple recurrent baseline and a longer-history baseline. Second, clarify the preprocessing pipeline to rule out leakage and provide pseudocode. Third, analyze robustness over longer unrolled sequences and quantify error accumulation in the trajectory memory stream. Fourth, provide more direct evidence that the scene context stream helps with partial observability or out-of-view context, perhaps by stratifying results by occlusion or map crop change. Fifth, make the latency comparison more transparent by separating benchmark-time and deployment-time costs. Finally, revise the claims to more carefully distinguish between improvements due to data reorganization and improvements due to the proposed temporal streams.

In summary, I think this is a good paper with a strong motivation, solid empirical results, and a practically relevant perspective. Its main weakness is that the current experimental design does not fully isolate the source of gains, and the “continuous driving” setting is still a synthetic proxy built from standard benchmarks. If the authors can better control for these issues and clarify the methodology, the work would be significantly stronger. As it stands, I view it as a promising and worthwhile contribution, but one that needs more rigorous validation of its central claims.

This paper addresses an important and underexplored mismatch between standard motion forecasting benchmarks and the way forecasting is actually used in autonomous driving systems. Rather than treating each scene independently, the paper argues that forecasting should be modeled in a continuous driving setting, where successive scenes are temporally linked and prior scene context and prior predictions can be reused. To this end, the authors propose RealMotion, which combines a scene context stream that propagates historical scene information across time and an agent trajectory stream that relays and refines predictions using a trajectory memory bank. The paper also introduces a data reorganization strategy that converts existing benchmark scenes into continuous sub-scene sequences. Overall, I found the paper timely, well motivated, and technically meaningful. The central idea is compelling: current forecasting pipelines indeed operate repeatedly online, and exploiting continuity across successive forecasting calls is a natural and practically relevant direction.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the problem formulation itself. The paper identifies a genuine limitation of the dominant benchmark protocol, namely the assumption that each forecasting instance is isolated. This is clearly illustrated in Figure 1 on page 2, where the contrast between independent scene processing and recurrent accumulation of historical information is intuitive and convincing. The motivating example of an occluded pedestrian and yielding behavior is especially effective in conveying why temporal continuity can matter beyond simply adding more history frames. This framing is not merely rhetorical; it leads to a concrete modeling and evaluation setup that better reflects deployment conditions. In that sense, the paper makes a valuable conceptual contribution in addition to an algorithmic one.

The proposed method is also well structured. The architecture in Figure 3 on page 4 is easy to follow and decomposes the approach into understandable parts. The scene context stream is a sensible mechanism for carrying forward encoded scene-level information after alignment into the current coordinate frame. The use of separate map-map and agent-scene cross-attention is a reasonable design choice, and the distinction between static map enrichment and dynamic agent-context aggregation is intuitive. Likewise, the agent trajectory stream is a thoughtful addition: instead of directly decoding from stale historical features, the method stores predicted trajectories and associated mode features in a memory bank, aligns them to the current frame, and uses them to refine current predictions. This is a practically grounded design that acknowledges the nonstationarity of local coordinate systems in forecasting. The trajectory embedding used to compare current and historical predictions is simple but effective.

Another notable strength is that the paper does not rely on an excessively complicated backbone. The encoder-decoder is intentionally plain, following prior work, which helps isolate the contribution of the continuous-driving formulation and the two temporal streams. This makes the empirical gains more convincing, because they are less likely to be attributable to a stronger base architecture alone. I also appreciated the inclusion of RealMotion-I as an independent variant without the continuous data reorganization or stream modules. That baseline is important for disentangling the effect of the proposed setting from the effect of the architecture.

The empirical results are strong. On the Argoverse 2 test set in Table 1 on page 6, RealMotion achieves the best reported minFDE1, minADE1, MR6, and b-minFDE6 among the listed methods, and is highly competitive on minFDE6/minADE6 as well. The improvement over QCNet on minFDE1 and minADE1 is substantial. The Argoverse 1 validation results in Table 2 on page 7 are also competitive, with the best minADE6 and tied-best MR6, though minFDE6 is slightly behind HPNet. The multi-agent results in Table 3 on page 7 are particularly encouraging given that the method is not primarily specialized for joint multi-agent forecasting; RealMotion still outperforms the listed baselines by a clear margin. The efficiency analysis in Table 6 on page 9 is another positive point: the model is relatively small and has favorable online latency compared with QCNet, which strengthens the practical relevance of the work.
