Proposition 4.2 formalizes the reduced-oscillation intuition by arguing that once ESPO enters the relaxed safe region, it can remain there and continue at least partial reward optimization, unlike CRPO which may revert to pure cost updates more often. Proposition 4.3 then argues that the adaptive sample manipulation yields fewer samples than a non-adaptive counterpart for achieving target reward/cost gaps. Even though the theory is restricted to the tabular setting, it is still valuable because it gives a principled foundation for a design choice that is usually treated heuristically in deep RL papers.

The empirical section is also fairly convincing at a high level. On Safety-MuJoCo, the plots on page 8 and the additional results on page 28 suggest that ESPO improves reward while keeping costs under control, and does so with fewer samples than CRPO and PCRPO. The sample counts in Table 1 are notable: 5.7M vs 8M on SafetyReacher-v4, 6.2M vs 8M on SafetyWalker-v4, and 5.1M vs 8M on SafetyHumanoidStandup-v4. On Omnisafe, the comparisons against PCPO, CUP, and PPOLag in Figure 3 and Table 2 are similarly encouraging, with ESPO using 7.3M/7.6M samples versus 10M for the baselines on the two reported tasks. The training-time reductions shown in the bar charts are also practically relevant. I also appreciated the ablation section and the update-style analysis in Table 3 on page 28, which supports the claim that ESPO spends many more updates in reward or reward-cost modes than CRPO.

That said, there are several issues that should be addressed to strengthen the paper.

My main concern is that the theoretical claims around sample efficiency are not yet as rigorous as the presentation suggests. Proposition 4.3 depends on Assumption A.7 in the appendix, which posits a particular relation between policy-evaluation error and sample size. This assumption is only qualitatively motivated and appears to be introduced specifically to make the adaptive-sampling argument go through. As written, the proposition is more of a conditional argument than a fully derived sample complexity theorem. Since sample efficiency is one of the headline contributions, the paper should be more explicit in the main text that this result relies on an additional assumption beyond the convergence theorem. Ideally, the authors would either derive the dependence from a standard concentration result in their setting or soften the wording around “provable sample efficiency.”

A second concern is a mismatch between the theory and the practical algorithm. The theory is developed for tabular softmax policies with approximate NPG-style updates, whereas the experiments are on continuous-control deep RL benchmarks with neural networks and PPO/PCPO/CUP-style baselines. This gap is common in RL papers, but here it matters because the adaptive sampling mechanism is the main novelty, and its behavior may depend strongly on noisy gradient estimates in high-dimensional function approximation. The paper would benefit from a clearer explanation of how gradients are estimated in practice, how the angle theta_{r,c} is computed robustly, and whether the sample-size adaptation itself introduces instability in deep settings. The practical algorithm in Appendix B is somewhat underspecified in this regard.

Relatedly, there seems to be some inconsistency in the algorithm description around Equations (3) and (4). In Section 4.1, Equation (3) is described as the projected update used when theta_{r,c} > 90 degrees, and Equation (4) as the weighted sum used when theta_{r,c} <= 90 degrees. However, in Section 4.3 and Algorithm 1, the mapping between angle conditions and update equations appears reversed in places. For example, page 5 states that for soft constraint violations with gradient angle <= 90 degrees, the policy is updated according to Equation (3), and for angle > 90 degrees according to Equation (4), which contradicts the earlier description. This is likely a presentation bug rather than a conceptual flaw, but it is important because it affects reproducibility and interpretation.

There are also some ambiguities in the sample-size adaptation rule itself. Equations (6) and (7) define Xt+1 = X + X zeta_t^+ or X + X zeta_t^- depending on conflict, but it is not fully clear whether X is a fixed base batch size reset every iteration or whether Xt evolves recursively over time. The notation suggests recursion, but the formula uses X rather than Xt. Algorithm 1 also refers to iterative changes in zeta_t^+ and zeta_t^- without much justification for those schedules. Since the empirical gains depend heavily on these mechanics, the paper should explain them more carefully and perhaps provide pseudocode with exact rollout-budget updates.

The experimental evaluation is promising but still somewhat limited in breadth and statistical depth. The paper reports results on a modest number of tasks, and although it mentions using at least three random seeds on page 29, the plots do not clearly indicate variance bars or confidence intervals in a way that supports strong statistical conclusions. Given the variability of safe RL, especially on MuJoCo-style tasks, it would be helpful to report mean ± standard deviation over more seeds and perhaps aggregate metrics such as normalized regret, cumulative constraint violation, or area under the reward-cost curve. In addition, because ESPO is compared across two different benchmark suites with somewhat different safety definitions, a more unified evaluation protocol would make the empirical story cleaner.

Another issue is fairness of comparison and implementation detail. The paper compares against both primal and primal-dual methods, which is useful, but the training-time comparisons may be influenced by implementation differences, hardware, and framework overhead. The authors do acknowledge on page 9 that sample reduction does not necessarily translate directly to time reduction because of benchmark characteristics and parallel processing. Still, if training time is emphasized as a key result, the paper should more carefully normalize for implementation factors or focus more on environment interactions, which are the more standard measure in RL. Also, ESPO is implemented inside Omnisafe for some comparisons, but it is not entirely clear whether all baselines were re-tuned equally under the same compute budget and whether the chosen hyperparameters are optimal for each method in the tested tasks.

I also think the paper could do a better job clarifying novelty relative to PCRPO. Conceptually, ESPO appears to combine PCRPO’s three-mode gradient handling with an adaptive sample-size rule based on gradient conflict. That is a meaningful extension, but the paper sometimes presents the contribution as broader than it is. In particular, the optimization logic itself is not new, and some of the theoretical analysis seems to inherit heavily from CRPO/PCRPO proof templates. This is not a problem, but the paper should more sharply distinguish what is genuinely new: the conflict-aware sampling criterion, the oscillation interpretation, and the adaptation of the analysis to this setting.

There are also a number of writing and notation issues throughout the paper. Several typos and grammatical errors appear in the main text and appendix. Some notation is overloaded or inconsistent, especially around Br/Bc/Bsoft and the naming of “Safety Violation Response” versus “No Violation Response” on page 5. The appendix contains a few likely typographical mistakes in equations and references to equation numbers. These do not invalidate the work, but they make the theory harder to verify than necessary.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper has real merit. The central idea is simple, relevant, and plausibly useful beyond the specific algorithm studied here. The empirical results are strong enough to suggest that the method is not merely a theoretical curiosity, and the attempt to connect adaptive sampling with reward-safety gradient geometry is original. I especially like that the paper targets a practical bottleneck in safe RL—wasted interactions under fixed rollout budgets—rather than only proposing another constrained optimizer. If the authors can tighten the exposition, resolve the equation/algorithm inconsistencies, and better qualify the theoretical sample-efficiency claim, this would be a solid contribution.

In summary, this is a good paper on an important problem. Its main strengths are a novel conflict-aware adaptive sampling idea for safe RL, a thoughtful integration with three-mode primal optimization, meaningful theoretical analysis in the tabular setting, and strong empirical improvements in reward, safety, sample usage, and training time on standard benchmarks. Its main weaknesses are the gap between theory and deep-RL practice, some ambiguity and inconsistency in the algorithm description, and limited rigor in the sample-efficiency theorem relative to how strongly it is advertised. I view these as addressable issues rather than fatal flaws. My overall assessment is positive, and I would lean toward acceptance if the authors can clarify the presentation and strengthen the empirical/theoretical alignment.

A few concrete suggestions for improvement are: explicitly fix the inconsistency between Equations (3)/(4) and Algorithm 1; clarify whether sample size is updated recursively and how zeta schedules are chosen; report more seeds and statistical summaries; include an ablation isolating the effect of adaptive sampling from the three-mode update logic; compare against a simpler adaptive-batch baseline based on variance or uncertainty rather than gradient conflict; and discuss computational overhead from estimating both reward and cost gradients and their angle each iteration. These additions would make the paper significantly stronger and easier to trust and reproduce.

This paper proposes GraphMETRO, a graph OOD generalization method aimed at handling complex, heterogeneous, and instance-specific distribution shifts. The core idea is to model unknown graph shifts as mixtures of predefined stochastic transformation classes, and to learn a mixture-of-experts architecture in which a gating network predicts which shift components are active while expert encoders produce “referentially invariant” representations aligned to a reference encoder. The method is evaluated on four real-world datasets from GOOD and several synthetic graph benchmarks, with reported gains over ERM and prior graph OOD baselines, especially on WebKB and Twitch.

Overall, I find the paper interesting and ambitious. The problem setting is important: graph OOD work often assumes a small number of environments or a single known shift type, whereas real graph shifts are indeed heterogeneous, compositional, and often instance-dependent. The paper’s attempt to move beyond fixed environment partitions and instead infer per-instance mixtures of shift components is conceptually appealing. The empirical results on GOOD are strong, especially the large gain on WebKB, and the method is presented as applicable to both node- and graph-level tasks. The paper also includes useful ablations on alignment and expert sharing, and the invariance-matrix analysis on page 9 is a nice attempt to inspect whether experts specialize as intended.

That said, I also have substantial concerns, mainly around the soundness of the theoretical claims, the dependence of the method on hand-designed transformation classes, and the extent to which the experiments really validate the central claim of handling “complex natural shifts” rather than benefiting from a more expressive architecture plus augmentation-like supervision. My overall assessment is positive but cautious: the empirical idea is promising, but the paper currently overstates its theoretical grounding and generality.

The main strengths are as follows. First, the paper addresses a genuinely important gap in graph OOD generalization. The motivation in the introduction, including the example in Figure 1 on page 1 and the decomposition illustration in Figure 2 on page 2, is compelling. The authors correctly point out that real-world graph shifts are not well captured by a small set of discrete environments or by single synthetic perturbations. Second, the proposed architecture is intuitive and reasonably novel in the graph OOD context. Using a gating model to infer instance-specific shift mixtures and experts to counteract specific shift components is a natural and potentially powerful design. Third, the alignment idea is practically important: without some shared representation anchor, aggregating expert outputs could indeed be unstable. The ablation in Appendix D.2, where removing alignment causes a large drop on WebKB, supports that this component matters. Fourth, the empirical performance is strong on the selected real-world benchmarks. Table 1 on page 7 shows consistent improvements over a broad set of baselines, including methods that do and do not require domain labels. Fifth, the paper makes a reasonable effort at interpretability through the gating outputs and invariance matrix, rather than treating the MoE as a black box.

My biggest concern is the theoretical section in Appendix A. The paper’s main text is mostly empirical and methodological, which is fine, but Appendix A presents “theoretical guarantees” that do not appear rigorous enough and in places seem incorrect. Theorem 1 assumes that after applying shift component tau_i, the gating model effectively selects only expert i, leading to h(tau_i(G)) = h(G). But the actual aggregation in Equation 2 is a softmax-weighted combination over all experts, not a hard selector, and no assumption or proof is given that all non-i weights vanish. Even if the gating model predicts the correct component, Equation 10 in the proof effectively replaces the weighted sum by a single term without justification. Theorem 2 then builds on this shaky result. Theorem 3 is more problematic: it invokes convexity/Jensen arguments in a way that does not seem valid for the stated model, and it claims the training objective upper-bounds target risk because training considers a “wider range” of transformations than the target distribution, which is not formally established. Also, the checklist says “NA” for theory, despite Appendix A containing explicit theorems and proofs. I would strongly recommend either removing these claims or substantially revising them into clearly labeled intuition/proof sketches with correct assumptions. As written, the theory weakens the paper.

A second major concern is the reliance on predefined stochastic transform functions as the basis of shift decomposition. This is both the method’s key design choice and its main limitation. The paper is commendably honest about this in Appendix F, but the main claims in the abstract and introduction are broader than what is actually demonstrated. GraphMETRO does not decompose arbitrary unknown shifts in a learned or identifiable way; rather, it decomposes them into mixtures over a user-specified library of transformations. If the true target shift is not well approximated by that library, the method may fail. This is especially important because the real-world GOOD datasets involve natural domain shifts, not synthetic perturbations, and the connection between those shifts and the chosen transforms is indirect. The paper argues that the discovered mixtures align qualitatively with dataset structure, but this remains suggestive rather than conclusive. In other words, the method is best understood as “robustness via a transformation basis and aligned experts,” not as a general solution to arbitrary complex graph shifts.

Relatedly, I am not fully convinced that the gains come specifically from correct shift decomposition rather than from a combination of increased model capacity, multi-view training, and transformation-based supervision. GraphMETRO uses multiple encoders, synthetic transformed samples, a gating auxiliary task, and an alignment loss. This is a substantial increase in inductive bias and capacity relative to ERM and many baselines. The paper does compare against ERM-Aug on synthetic datasets, which is helpful, but there is no equally direct comparison on the real-world datasets to a strong augmentation baseline using the same transform library and similar compute budget. Such a comparison would be very important. Otherwise, it is hard to isolate whether the MoE decomposition itself is the source of improvement. The ablation “GraphMETRO without L1” in Table 4 helps somewhat, but it removes the gating supervision entirely rather than comparing against simpler alternatives such as uniform averaging over experts, single-expert augmentation training, or a non-expert multi-branch ensemble with the same number of parameters.

The experimental section is generally solid, but there are several issues that limit interpretability. First, the real-world evaluation in Table 1 mixes baselines across node and graph tasks, and some entries are NA because methods are task-specific. That is understandable, but it makes the comparison landscape uneven. More importantly, the strongest baseline on WebKB and Twitch appears to be EERM, but it would help to know whether all methods were tuned comparably under the same backbone and hyperparameter budget. The paper states that most baseline results come from GOOD, except Twitter, while GraphMETRO uses its own grid search over learning rates. This is common practice, but because the reported gain on WebKB is very large, stronger reassurance about fair tuning would be useful. Second, the reported p-values in Table 1 are welcome, but the paper does not clearly specify the statistical test used. Third, the number of runs is only five for GraphMETRO, and some standard deviations are fairly large, especially on WebKB. The improvement is still large there, but more runs would strengthen confidence.

I also have some methodological questions about the training objective and formulation. Equation 3 defines L1 using BCE on the ground-truth mixture labels Y(tau^(k)), which are available only because the training transformations are synthetically generated. This means the gating model is not discovering latent shift components from source data alone; it is supervised to recognize the authors’ chosen transform classes. That is perfectly valid, but it should be described more explicitly as supervised transformation recognition rather than unsupervised shift decomposition. Similarly, the claim that the method handles “unknown” shifts should be qualified: it handles unknown mixtures over known transformation classes. Also, the notation around tau^(k)-invariance is somewhat loose. The paper suggests that training on compositions of transforms enforces invariance to multiple shifts, but this depends heavily on the sampled compositions and on the gating model’s ability to recognize them. The practical success may be real, but the conceptual claim should be stated more carefully.

The notion of “referential invariant representation” is interesting, but I think the paper could explain it more clearly and more modestly. As defined on page 5, expert xi is trained so that xi(tau_i(G)) approximates xi_0(G), where xi_0 is the reference model on the original graph. This is less a classical invariant representation and more a transformation-aligned representation relative to a reference encoder. That is a useful idea, but the terminology may overstate what is guaranteed. In particular, if the reference encoder itself is not robust, then aligning transformed inputs to its outputs may preserve source-domain biases. Some discussion of why the reference model is a good anchor, and whether it should be frozen or jointly trained, would help. The paper seems to train it jointly as part of the expert set, which raises the possibility of drift in the anchor space.

The interpretability claims are promising but currently limited. Figure 4(b) on page 9 shows average mixture weights on WebKB and Twitch, and the authors argue these align with dataset structure. However, the mapping from transforms like “add edges” or “drop node” to real domain shifts such as university-domain or language shifts is not straightforward. For example, why should “add edges” dominate WebKB? Is there empirical evidence that target domains are denser, or is this simply the transform that best helps the model? Likewise, the gating model’s high accuracy at identifying synthetic mixtures does not necessarily imply that its outputs on natural target data correspond to true underlying shifts. I appreciate that the authors acknowledge the difficulty of quantitative validation here, but then the interpretability claims should be toned down.

There are also some clarity and presentation issues. The paper is generally readable, but several claims are repeated in a somewhat inflated way, especially around being “the first” to address complex graph shifts. I would encourage more precise positioning. The computational complexity discussion on page 7 states training complexity O(K^2 |D_s|), but this is fairly coarse and does not reflect backbone cost, graph size, or batching; a more practical runtime/memory comparison would be more useful. The appendix mentions GPU information in the checklist, but I did not see a concrete compute table in the provided pages. Since the method uses multiple encoders, reporting wall-clock overhead versus ERM would be valuable. Also, the paper excludes molecular GOOD datasets because they require domain-specific transform design; this is reasonable, but it further underscores that the method’s applicability depends on transform engineering.

I think the paper would be significantly stronger with the following revisions or additional experiments. First, remove or substantially rewrite the theoretical appendix. At minimum, the current theorems should not be presented as formal guarantees. Second, add a stronger real-world baseline using the same transform library but without MoE decomposition, for example ERM-Aug or a single encoder trained on all transformed samples with the same alignment-free objective budget. Third, include a parameter-matched or compute-matched comparison to test whether gains come from MoE specialization rather than simply more capacity. Fourth, provide more analysis of gating behavior on real data: per-domain mixture distributions, calibration, and whether gating weights correlate with measurable graph statistics such as degree, graph size, or feature noise proxies. Fifth, clarify whether the reference encoder is frozen or jointly optimized, and analyze sensitivity to that choice. Sixth, if possible, include experiments where the target shift is intentionally outside the transform library, to test robustness to basis mismatch. That would directly probe the central assumption.

Despite these concerns, I do think the paper has merit. The empirical results are strong, the problem is important, and the proposed architecture is a meaningful step toward more adaptive graph OOD methods. My main reservation is that the paper currently oversells the generality and theoretical grounding of what is, in essence, a supervised transformation-basis MoE framework. If the claims were tightened and the evaluation better isolated the source of gains, I would view the contribution more favorably.

In summary, this is a promising and practically relevant paper with a novel graph OOD architecture and strong benchmark results, but it has notable weaknesses in theoretical rigor, claim calibration, and experimental disentanglement. I would lean positive on the basis of empirical contribution and originality, but only if the authors address the overclaiming and clarify the method’s actual scope.

This paper proposes GraphMETRO, a graph out-of-distribution generalization method aimed at handling complex, heterogeneous, and instance-dependent distribution shifts. The central idea is to model unknown target shifts as mixtures of predefined stochastic graph transformations, and then learn a mixture-of-experts architecture in which a gating network predicts which shift components are active while expert networks produce “referentially invariant” representations aligned to a shared reference model. The method is evaluated on both real-world datasets from the GOOD benchmark and synthetic shift settings, with additional analyses on invariance and shift discovery.

Overall, I found the paper interesting, ambitious, and quite compelling. The problem setting is important: graph OOD work often assumes relatively simple or homogeneous shifts, whereas real graph data can exhibit multiple simultaneous and instance-specific changes. The paper’s main contribution is to explicitly embrace this complexity rather than forcing all shifts into a single invariant predictor. The proposed decomposition into shift components, together with a gating mechanism and aligned experts, is a thoughtful and original design. Empirically, the method appears strong, especially on the real-world GOOD datasets, where the gains on WebKB are particularly striking. In my view, this is a meaningful contribution to graph OOD generalization and a paper that should be taken seriously.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the framing. The authors identify a real limitation in prior graph OOD methods: many either rely on fixed augmentation families, assume a small number of environments, or seek a single invariant representation that may be too rigid under heterogeneous shifts. The motivating examples in the introduction and Figure 1 are effective, and the high-level decomposition shown in Figure 2 on page 2 makes the intuition clear. The idea that different target instances may be affected by different combinations of shift factors is both realistic and underexplored in graph learning. This gives the paper a strong conceptual foundation.

Methodologically, the paper is also quite elegant. The use of a gating model to infer instance-specific shift mixtures and expert models to mitigate individual shift components is natural, but the key addition is the alignment mechanism through the reference model. Without such alignment, aggregating expert outputs would indeed be unstable or semantically incoherent. The notion of “referential invariant representation” is a useful way to formalize this. The training objective in Equation 3 is simple enough to implement yet captures the intended behavior: the gating model is supervised using synthetic mixtures of transformations, while the experts and classifier are trained to both predict labels and align transformed representations to the reference representation. This is a nice design, and the ablations later support that the alignment term is not cosmetic but essential.

The empirical results on real-world datasets are impressive. Table 1 on page 7 shows consistent improvements over a broad set of baselines, including ERM, domain generalization methods, and graph-specific OOD methods. The WebKB result is especially notable: 41.11 ± 7.47 versus the strongest baseline at 24.61 ± 4.86. Even allowing for the relatively high variance, this is a large margin. The gains on Twitch and the graph classification datasets are smaller but still favorable. I also appreciate that the method is evaluated on both node- and graph-level tasks, which supports the claim of generality better than many graph OOD papers that focus on only one setting.

The synthetic experiments are also useful, not because they are the main evidence, but because they help unpack what the method is doing. Figure 3 on page 8 and the numerical tables in Appendix E show that GraphMETRO is often stronger than both ERM and ERM with augmentation under single and composed shifts. This is important because the method is not merely doing standard augmentation; it is learning to decompose and mitigate shifts. The invariance matrix in Figure 4(a) on page 9 is a particularly nice diagnostic: it gives evidence that experts specialize in the intended way. Likewise, the shift-mixture visualizations in Figure 4(b) are a valuable interpretability angle and make the paper more insightful than a purely predictive benchmark paper.

I also want to credit the paper for being fairly complete experimentally. The appendices include architecture details, hyperparameters, transform libraries, and ablations on shared-vs-separate experts, alignment removal, and number of transform functions. The ablation in Table 5 on page 21 is especially convincing: removing alignment causes a substantial drop, which validates a central design choice. The discussion in Appendix F is also refreshingly honest about the dependence on transform design and gating quality.

That said, there are several issues that should be addressed or at least clarified.

My main concern is the gap between the motivating claim—handling natural, unknown, complex real-world shifts—and the actual supervision used to train the gating model and experts. The method depends critically on a predefined library of stochastic transform functions, and the gating model is trained to recognize mixtures of these synthetic transforms. This means the success of the approach hinges on whether the chosen transforms span the relevant shift directions in the target domain. The paper acknowledges this limitation in Appendix F, but it remains central. In some sense, GraphMETRO is only as good as its shift basis. This does not invalidate the contribution, but the paper should be more explicit in the main text that the method is not shift-agnostic; it is shift-basis-dependent. The strong real-world results suggest the chosen transforms are useful, but it would help to better articulate why these particular transforms are expected to capture the GOOD benchmark shifts.

Relatedly, the choice of transform functions seems somewhat heuristic. The paper uses common graph augmentations such as random subgraph sampling, edge dropping, node dropping, feature noise, and edge addition. These are reasonable, but the connection between each transform and each real-world dataset’s actual shift mechanism is not always tight. For example, for WebKB and Twitch, the interpretation in Figure 4(b) is interesting, but still somewhat speculative. The paper itself notes that quantitatively validating these discovered shifts remains challenging. I think this is acceptable for now, but the interpretability claims should be phrased carefully: the method discovers mixtures over the chosen transform basis, not necessarily the true causal shift factors.

A second concern is computational cost and scalability. The paper states on page 7 that the forward process requires O(K) encoder passes and training complexity scales as O(K^2 |Ds|) because of extrapolation. This is nontrivial, especially if one wants a richer transform library or larger graphs. The appendix includes a shared-encoder variant, but it performs worse. Since MoE is often motivated by efficiency, it is worth emphasizing that this is not a sparse conditional-computation MoE in the usual sense; it is closer to an ensemble of experts whose outputs are all aggregated. I would have liked to see wall-clock training time, GPU memory, or parameter count comparisons against baselines. This is especially important because some of the gains may partly come from increased model capacity due to multiple encoders. The synthetic experiments hint at this possibility when in-distribution performance sometimes improves. A stronger capacity-controlled comparison would make the empirical claims even more convincing.

A third issue is the theoretical appendix. I do not think the paper needs theory to be valuable, but the current theoretical section is not fully convincing. In particular, Theorem 1 appears to rely on idealized gating behavior and effectively assumes away contributions from non-selected experts. Equation (10) is a strong simplification that does not obviously follow from the soft weighting in Equation 2. Theorem 2 then builds on this approximation. The generalization bound in Theorem 3 is also quite informal and seems to make several leaps, including assumptions about the target distribution being representable by the training transform family and about the training objective covering a “wider range” of transformations. I would therefore not treat the theory as a rigorous guarantee. My suggestion would be either to substantially tighten the assumptions and proofs or to present this section more explicitly as intuition rather than formal theory. This is a fixable presentation issue, but it is worth noting.

There are also some experimental questions. First, the comparison set is broad, but not always perfectly matched across tasks, and some baselines are unavailable on some datasets. That is understandable, but it makes the strongest claims somewhat dependent on the benchmark setup. Second, the number of runs for GraphMETRO is five, while some baseline numbers are inherited from GOOD; it would be useful to know whether all methods were rerun under identical conditions for the newly added Twitter dataset and whether variance across seeds is comparable. Third, the p-values in Table 1 are appreciated, but the paper does not fully specify the statistical test used. This is a minor reproducibility detail that should be easy to add.

I also think the paper could do a better job disentangling the contributions of decomposition, gating, and extra capacity. For example, a useful baseline would be a multi-expert model without gating but with uniform averaging, or a model with the same number of parameters trained on all augmentations jointly. The ablation “without L1” partially addresses the gating supervision, but not the broader question of whether the gains come from conditional specialization versus simply having multiple encoders. Similarly, a top-1 expert selection variant versus soft aggregation could be informative.

Despite these concerns, I view them as opportunities to strengthen an already strong paper rather than fundamental flaws. The core idea is novel and well motivated, the method is technically coherent, and the empirical results are genuinely impressive on challenging real-world graph OOD benchmarks. The paper also offers useful interpretability and diagnostic analyses beyond raw accuracy tables. In a space where many methods either assume too much structure or rely on narrow augmentation schemes, this work pushes toward a more realistic and flexible treatment of graph distribution shifts.

To improve the paper further, I would recommend the following. First, move some of the limitation discussion from Appendix F into the main paper, especially the dependence on transform design and gating quality. Second, either strengthen or soften the theoretical claims. Third, add explicit compute and parameter comparisons, and if possible include one or two capacity-matched ablations to isolate the benefit of the MoE decomposition from model size. Fourth, clarify the statistical testing protocol and, if space permits, include a brief discussion of how transform families were selected for each dataset. Finally, it would be helpful to discuss whether the method could be extended to learn or adapt the transform basis rather than fixing it manually.

In summary, this is a strong paper with a fresh perspective on graph OOD generalization. Its central idea—modeling unknown graph shifts as mixtures of aligned expert-handled components—is both intuitive and technically interesting, and the empirical evidence is strong enough to make the contribution credible. While some assumptions are important and the theory is less solid than the experiments, I believe the paper advances the field in a meaningful way and would be a positive addition to the conference.

My recommendation is acceptance.

This paper studies the approximation quality of Bayesian coresets through general upper and lower bounds on the KL divergence between the full posterior and a coreset posterior. The main contribution is a fairly broad theoretical framework that goes beyond prior analyses restricted to exponential families or strongly log-concave/smooth posteriors. The paper derives lower bounds under mild local asymptotic assumptions and upper bounds under a generalized subexponentiality condition on the log-likelihood contributions. It then uses these results to explain why importance-weighted coresets can perform poorly and why subsample-optimize methods can succeed with polylogarithmic coreset size. The paper also includes empirical illustrations on two deliberately challenging models: a multimodal, unidentifiable Cauchy location model and an unidentifiable heavy-tailed logistic regression model.

Overall, I found the paper strong. The problem is important, the results are nontrivial, and the paper makes a meaningful conceptual advance in the theory of Bayesian coresets. In particular, the lower bounds seem especially valuable: they provide a principled explanation for a long-standing empirical observation that naive importance-weighted subsampling often fails badly for posterior approximation. The upper-bound side is also useful, though somewhat more assumption-heavy and less immediately sharp in practice. The work is mathematically sophisticated, and the proofs in the appendix appear careful and substantial.

The main strength of the paper is its scope relative to prior theory. The introduction clearly motivates that many scalable Bayesian inference guarantees rely on asymptotic normality, unimodality, or strong log-concavity, whereas coreset methods are often empirically useful precisely in settings where those assumptions fail. The paper addresses this gap directly. The lower-bound machinery in Section 3 is elegant: Lemma 3.1 reduces KL lower bounding to a localized overlap quantity over a set B, and Theorems 3.3 and 3.5 then translate posterior approximation difficulty into statements about weighted sums of score vectors and local curvature. This reduction is conceptually clean and likely useful beyond the specific corollaries proved here.

A second major strength is that the theory leads to concrete algorithmic insights rather than remaining purely abstract. Corollaries 4.1 and 4.2 show that importance-weighted coresets require coreset size scaling essentially linearly with N to maintain bounded KL, even after optimal post-hoc scaling. This is a strong and practically relevant negative result. Corollary 4.3 gives a dimension-dependent impossibility result for any coreset construction with fewer than d points under suitable conditions. On the positive side, Corollary 6.1 gives a broad justification for subsample-optimize methods, showing bounded KL with M of polylogarithmic order under alignment and subexponentiality assumptions. This balance of negative and positive results makes the paper much more compelling.

The empirical section, while limited in scope, is well chosen. The two models in Eqs. (2) and (3) are not toy examples in the sense of being overly favorable to the theory; rather, they are intentionally difficult cases with multimodality, unidentifiability, and heavy tails. The plots on page 8 (Figure 2) support the predicted scaling laws for importance-weighted coresets and optimally scaled variants, and the plots on page 10 (Figure 3) show that subsample-optimize coresets can indeed achieve very small KL with logarithmic-size coresets in these settings. These experiments are aligned with the paper’s claims and help validate that the asymptotic theory is not vacuous.

That said, I do have several concerns and suggestions.

My main reservation is about the practical interpretability of the upper-bound assumptions. The lower bounds are relatively satisfying because they rely on assumptions that resemble standard local asymptotic conditions. By contrast, the upper bounds hinge on Definition 5.2, namely (h, A)-subexponentiality of the centered log-likelihood vector under the posterior. While Proposition 5.4 shows this holds locally whenever the posterior moment generating function exists in a neighborhood of zero, the resulting constant beta is existential and model-dependent. Similarly, Corollary 6.1 depends on the alignment probability condition in Eq. (6), which is intuitive but not easy to verify generically. The paper acknowledges this limitation in the conclusion, but I think the presentation could do more to help readers understand when these assumptions are likely to hold with favorable constants and when they may be too weak to be predictive. As written, the upper-bound theory is broad but somewhat difficult to operationalize.

Relatedly, Corollary 6.1 is interesting but feels less definitive than the lower-bound results. The statement depends on three ingredients: subexponentiality with increasing probability, polynomial growth of Var_pi(ell), and the alignment condition. The last condition is especially central, yet it is not directly tied to a concrete sampling scheme beyond the generic probabilities p_n. Since the practical success of Algorithm 3 depends heavily on how the subsample is chosen, it would strengthen the paper if the authors could discuss more explicitly what classes of sampling distributions are expected to satisfy Eq. (6), even heuristically. For example, are uniform probabilities typically enough in redundant-data regimes, or is leverage-style sampling needed? The current theorem is useful as a framework, but its algorithmic implications remain somewhat indirect.

A second concern is that the paper defines coreset quality using the minimum or maximum of forward and reverse KL in different sections. In Section 3, KL(w) is defined as the minimum of forward and reverse KL for lower bounds, while in Section 5 it is defined as the maximum for upper bounds. This is mathematically reasonable for the respective purposes, but it creates some notational friction and could confuse readers. I would strongly recommend using distinct notation, or at least emphasizing the switch more prominently. As it stands, a reader skimming the paper could easily miss that KL(w) changes meaning.

A third issue is that some of the assumptions in the lower-bound applications are stronger than the headline message may suggest. For example, Corollary 4.3 requires assumptions (A7) and (A8), including a linear independence/moment condition on gradients of selected points. This is fine, but the interpretation “any construction algorithm requires M > d” should be read locally and under these conditions, not as a universal information-theoretic lower bound for all models and all notions of coreset quality. The paper mostly states this carefully, but the prose around the contributions could be slightly more qualified to avoid overgeneralization.

I also think the experimental section could be expanded modestly. The current experiments are convincing as sanity checks for the asymptotic claims, but they are both synthetic and low-dimensional. Since one of the paper’s motivations is scalable Bayesian inference for large datasets, it would be helpful to include at least one more realistic example, even if still moderate in dimension, to show that the qualitative conclusions persist outside carefully constructed models. Alternatively, if the goal is purely theoretical validation, the paper could say this more explicitly. Right now the experiments are good but narrow.

On the technical side, the paper is generally well written, but some sections are dense enough that additional intuition would help. In particular, Theorems 3.3 and 3.5 are important but not easy to parse on first reading. A short informal interpretation immediately after each theorem would improve accessibility. For instance, after Theorem 3.3, the paper could explicitly say that bounded KL requires the coreset score average gw/w to match the full-data score average g/N to within order N^{-1/2}, up to curvature and localization terms. Likewise, after Theorem 5.3, it would help to emphasize more plainly that the KL is controlled by posterior variance of the log-likelihood residual when the subexponential condition holds. The appendix proofs are detailed, but the main text could do more to guide the reader.

I have a few more minor comments. First, the desiderata in Section 2 include coreset construction time o(N) or at most O(N) with a small constant, but some of the analyzed methods, especially those requiring nonuniform probabilities or posterior-based optimization surrogates, may not obviously satisfy this in practice. A brief discussion distinguishing statistical approximation guarantees from end-to-end computational savings would be useful. Second, the paper focuses exclusively on KL divergence; some discussion of whether similar techniques might extend to integral probability metrics or task-specific posterior expectation error would broaden the impact. Third, the figures are informative, but the captions could say a bit more about how KL was computed numerically in the heavy-tailed examples.

Despite these concerns, my overall assessment is positive. The paper makes a substantial theoretical contribution to the study of Bayesian coresets. The lower bounds are novel, insightful, and likely to influence how researchers think about coreset construction. The upper bounds are less sharp in a practical sense, but they still provide a meaningful unifying framework that covers settings beyond prior analyses. The empirical results, especially Figures 2 and 3 on pages 8 and 10, support the main qualitative claims. I would be inclined to accept this paper.

To strengthen the final version, I would encourage the authors to do three things. First, clarify the practical meaning of the upper-bound assumptions, especially Eq. (6), perhaps with examples of sampling schemes or model classes where they are expected to hold. Second, clean up the KL notation so that lower- and upper-bound quantities are not denoted identically. Third, add a bit more intuition in the main text around the central theorems and, if space permits, one additional experiment or discussion point connecting the asymptotic theory to a more realistic application setting.

In summary, this is a rigorous and valuable paper. Its main contribution is not a new coreset algorithm but a general theory that explains both the limitations of importance-weighted constructions and the promise of subsample-optimize approaches in broad Bayesian models, including multimodal and heavy-tailed settings. That is an important contribution, and the paper advances the state of understanding in this area.

This paper studies the approximation quality of Bayesian coresets through general upper and lower bounds on KL divergence, with the explicit goal of moving beyond the restrictive assumptions that dominate prior theory. The central message is clear and important: while Bayesian coresets are empirically useful in a broad range of nonclassical posterior settings, the theory has lagged behind, and this paper substantially closes that gap. Overall, I found the paper technically strong, well motivated, and genuinely insightful. It makes a meaningful theoretical contribution to scalable Bayesian inference, and it does so in a way that also clarifies practical algorithmic consequences.

The main strengths are the breadth and sharpness of the theoretical results. On the lower-bound side, the paper develops general asymptotic KL lower bounds under assumptions that are much milder than those used in earlier coreset analyses. In particular, the results do not rely on exponential-family structure, strong log-concavity, or posterior normality in the usual global sense. Theorems 3.3 and 3.5 are the core contributions here: they reduce posterior approximation difficulty to properties of weighted sums of score-like quantities and local curvature, which is both elegant and useful. I especially appreciated that the lower bounds are not merely abstract impossibility statements; they are leveraged to derive concrete consequences for widely used construction strategies. The conclusion that importance-weighted coresets require coreset size proportional to dataset size to maintain bounded KL, and that even optimal post-hoc scaling only improves this to a logarithmic lower bound, is a strong and practically relevant negative result. Likewise, the dimension-dependent lower bound showing that any construction needs more than d points in locally d-parameter settings is conceptually clean and likely to be broadly cited.

The upper-bound side is also compelling. Lemma 5.1 gives a very general KL upper bound in terms of exponential moments under the true posterior, and Theorem 5.3 turns this into a usable criterion via the proposed multivariate subexponentiality condition. This is a nice abstraction: it is weaker and more flexible than the assumptions in prior work, yet still strong enough to yield interpretable guarantees. Proposition 5.4 is particularly valuable because it shows that this condition is not exotic; under local finiteness of the moment generating function, one obtains subexponentiality with covariance structure as the controlling matrix. This makes the framework feel principled rather than ad hoc. The application to subsample-optimize methods in Corollary 6.1 is then a satisfying payoff: the paper explains why these methods can succeed with polylogarithmic coreset size in a broad class of models, substantially extending prior positive theory.

A major virtue of the paper is that it does not stop at theorem statements but uses them to explain empirical phenomena that practitioners have observed for years. The analysis of importance-weighted constructions is a good example. These methods are simple and computationally attractive, but often disappointing in practice; the paper gives a convincing theoretical explanation for why. Conversely, the positive analysis of subsample-optimize methods aligns with recent empirical success and helps distinguish which algorithmic ingredients matter. This kind of theory-to-practice bridge is exactly what one hopes for in a mature theoretical ML paper.

The experimental section is modest in scale but well chosen and effective for validation. The two synthetic models are not generic toy examples; they are deliberately selected to violate assumptions common in the literature: the multimodal, unidentifiable Cauchy location model with heavy-tailed prior, and the unidentifiable logistic regression model with heavy-tailed prior and persistent posterior heavy tails. The posterior visualizations on page 6 are useful in conveying the pathologies of these settings, and Figures 2 and 3 provide direct empirical support for the theoretical claims. In particular, the scaling trends in Figure 2 match the predicted lower-bound behavior for importance-weighted methods, while Figure 3 shows that subsample-optimize constructions can indeed maintain very small KL with logarithmic coreset size. For a theory paper, this level of empirical validation is appropriate and convincing.

I also found the exposition generally strong. The paper is mathematically dense, but the high-level narrative is coherent: Section 3 develops lower bounds, Section 4 turns them into algorithmic consequences, Section 5 develops upper bounds, and Section 6 applies them to modern coreset constructions. The basic KL lower and upper lemmas are useful organizing devices. The proofs in the appendix appear careful and substantial, and the assumptions are stated explicitly. The paper also does a good job of clarifying what is and is not required by the theory. For example, the discussion around local concentration sets B and the avoidance of direct control over coreset-tail behavior is insightful.

That said, there are a few limitations and points where the paper could be improved. First, while the subexponentiality framework is elegant, its practical verifiability remains somewhat indirect. The paper acknowledges in the conclusion that both the subexponentiality constant in Proposition 5.4 and the alignment probability in Corollary 6.1 currently require case-by-case analysis. This is a real limitation because it leaves some gap between the general theorem and turnkey applicability. I do not view this as a serious flaw—the paper is already making a substantial advance—but it would strengthen the work if the authors could add more guidance, perhaps in the main text or appendix, on how one might verify these conditions in common model classes beyond the two examples considered.

Second, the empirical section is intentionally narrow and focused on validation rather than benchmarking. That is acceptable for a theory-first paper, but some readers may still want a slightly broader empirical picture. For example, it could be useful to include one additional experiment on a more standard identifiable model, not because the theory needs it, but to show continuity with classical settings and to help calibrate the practical magnitude of the bounds. Similarly, some discussion of how tight the upper bounds are in practice, relative to observed KL, would be informative.

Third, some assumptions in the lower-bound applications, especially the alignment and moment conditions used in the corollaries, are technically reasonable but may be hard for non-specialists to parse. The paper would benefit from a short intuition box or paragraph summarizing which assumptions are essentially standard asymptotic regularity conditions, which are algorithm-specific, and which are mainly proof artifacts. This would improve accessibility without changing the technical content.

I have a minor concern about the optimization oracle implicit in Algorithm 3. The algorithm is stated as minimizing KL over weights supported on a sampled subset, but in practice the experiments use nonnegative least squares on discretized log-likelihoods via posterior samples, as noted in the caption of Figure 3 on page 10. This is perfectly reasonable experimentally, but the relationship between the idealized optimization problem in the theorem and the practical surrogate used in experiments could be spelled out a bit more clearly. A brief discussion of whether the theory is intended to justify the idealized algorithm only, or also approximate implementations of it, would help.

Despite these relatively minor issues, my overall assessment is very positive. The paper addresses an important open problem in Bayesian coreset theory, introduces genuinely new techniques, and derives results that are both mathematically nontrivial and practically illuminating. The negative results for importance-weighted methods are especially valuable because they clarify a long-standing empirical puzzle, while the positive results for subsample-optimize methods provide a broad theoretical foundation for a promising class of algorithms. The work is original, rigorous, and likely to have lasting impact on the literature on scalable Bayesian inference.

In summary, I believe this is a strong paper. Its main contribution is not just another bound under slightly altered assumptions, but a substantial expansion of the theoretical scope of Bayesian coreset analysis, together with concrete algorithmic implications. I would be supportive of acceptance.
